# Systems and Hardware {#sec-appendix-systems}

This appendix provides the deterministic operating system and embedded hardware foundations that bridge high-latency AI accelerators with physical actuators. For machine learning systems engineers familiar with standard Linux environments, distributed cluster runtimes, and asynchronous task queues, it formalizes the real-time operating system bounds (PREEMPT_RT scheduling, interrupt partitioning, lock-free synchronization), deterministic communication fabrics (CAN-FD, EtherCAT, TSN), memory hierarchy and interconnect contention, power delivery networks, and electromechanical actuator dynamics used throughout this book, alongside the canonical wire formats of records crossing the proposal boundary. Each model and bound depends on a specified hardware substrate, execution workload, and operating envelope, identifying the exact physical invariants that must be verified before an autonomous action can be certified.

## How to Use This Appendix

Consult this appendix when diagnosing physical systems bottlenecks, timing jitter, electrical rail instability, or hardware interface boundaries across chapters in this book:

## Numbers to Know in Physical AI {#sec-appendix-systems-numbers-to-know}

```{python}
#| label: appendix-systems-numbers-to-know
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ NUMBERS TO KNOW IN PHYSICAL AI (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-appendix-systems-numbers-to-know, @tbl-numbers-rate-hierarchy,
# │          @tbl-numbers-kinematics, @tbl-numbers-edge-compute, @tbl-numbers-thermal,
# │          @tbl-numbers-safety, and @tbl-numbers-buses.
# │ Goal: Centralize foundational orders of magnitude across rate hierarchies,
# │       kinetic stopping, edge memory streaming, thermal dynamics, statistical safety,
# │       and real-time fieldbuses.
# │ Show: Formatted physical reference figures sourced directly from mlsysim.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import (
    fmt,
    fmt_int,
    fmt_frequency,
    fmt_latency,
    fmt_length,
    fmt_velocity,
    fmt_acceleration,
    fmt_percent,
    fmt_memory,
    fmt_params,
    fmt_bandwidth,
    check,
    MarkdownStr,
)
from decimal import Decimal, ROUND_HALF_UP

class PhysicalNumbersToKnow:
    """Namespace for physical AI reference numbers, rate hierarchies, and scaling laws."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────────────────────────────
    R = ReferenceStats.PhysicalAIRates
    K = ReferenceStats.PhysicalAIKinematics
    T = ReferenceStats.PhysicalAIThermal
    S = ReferenceStats.PhysicalAISafety
    B = ReferenceStats.PhysicalAIBuses
    C = ReferenceStats.PhysicalAICompute

    # Rates
    intent_lo = R.IntentLo
    intent_hi = R.IntentHi
    chunk_lo = R.ChunkLo
    chunk_hi = R.ChunkHi
    permission = R.PermissionRate
    current_lo = R.CurrentLoopLo
    current_hi = R.CurrentLoopHi
    switching_lo = R.GateSwitchingLo
    switching_hi = R.GateSwitchingHi

    # Kinematics & Platforms
    _MPS = meter / second
    _MPS2 = meter / second**2
    hum_v = 1.0 * _MPS
    hum_a = 4.0 * _MPS2
    rm_v = 1.5 * _MPS
    rm_a = 2.0 * _MPS2
    bot_v = 6.0 * _MPS
    bot_a = 4.5 * _MPS2
    av_v = 30.0 * _MPS
    av_a = 7.0 * _MPS2

    tau_50 = 50 * millisecond
    tau_200 = 200 * millisecond

    # Compute & Memory
    vla_params_7b = C.VlaParameters7B
    vla_params_14b = 14e9 * param
    dram_bw = C.EdgeMemorySustainedOrin
    chunk_horizon = C.VlaChunkHorizon

    # Safety
    rule_of_three = S.RuleOfThreeMultiplier
    lambda_asild = S.TargetFailureRateASILD
    lambda_sil3 = S.TargetFailureRateSIL3
    lambda_robotaxi = 1e-6 / hour

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    # Rates & Periods
    intent_t_lo = (1 / intent_hi).to(millisecond)
    intent_t_hi = (1 / intent_lo).to(millisecond)
    chunk_t_lo = (1 / chunk_hi).to(millisecond)
    chunk_t_hi = (1 / chunk_lo).to(millisecond)
    perm_t = (1 / permission).to(millisecond)
    curr_t_lo = (1 / current_hi).to(microsecond)
    curr_t_hi = (1 / current_lo).to(microsecond)
    sw_t_lo = (1 / switching_hi).to(microsecond)
    sw_t_hi = (1 / switching_lo).to(microsecond)

    # Kinematics
    hum_blind_50 = (hum_v * tau_50).to(millimeter)
    hum_blind_200 = (hum_v * tau_200).to(millimeter)
    hum_stop_200 = calc_safe_stopping_distance(hum_v, tau_200, hum_a).to(millimeter)
    hum_share_200 = (hum_blind_200 / hum_stop_200).to("dimensionless").magnitude

    rm_blind_50 = (rm_v * tau_50).to(millimeter)
    rm_blind_200 = (rm_v * tau_200).to(millimeter)
    rm_stop_200_raw = calc_safe_stopping_distance(rm_v, tau_200, rm_a).to(millimeter)
    rm_stop_200 = float(Decimal(repr(rm_stop_200_raw.magnitude)).quantize(Decimal("1"), rounding=ROUND_HALF_UP)) * millimeter
    rm_share_200 = (rm_blind_200 / rm_stop_200_raw).to("dimensionless").magnitude

    bot_blind_50 = (bot_v * tau_50).to(millimeter)
    bot_blind_200 = (bot_v * tau_200).to(meter)
    bot_stop_200 = calc_safe_stopping_distance(bot_v, tau_200, bot_a).to(meter)
    bot_share_200 = (bot_blind_200 / bot_stop_200).to("dimensionless").magnitude

    av_blind_50 = (av_v * tau_50).to(meter)
    av_blind_200 = (av_v * tau_200).to(meter)
    av_stop_200 = calc_safe_stopping_distance(av_v, tau_200, av_a).to(meter)
    av_share_200 = (av_blind_200 / av_stop_200).to("dimensionless").magnitude

    # Edge Compute (DRAM streaming time = Footprint / Sustained Bandwidth)
    fp16_bytes = 2 * byte / param
    int8_bytes = 1 * byte / param
    int4_bytes = 0.5 * byte / param

    footprint_7b_fp16 = (vla_params_7b * fp16_bytes).to(GB)
    footprint_7b_int8 = (vla_params_7b * int8_bytes).to(GB)
    footprint_7b_int4 = (vla_params_7b * int4_bytes).to(GB)
    footprint_14b_int8 = (vla_params_14b * int8_bytes).to(GB)

    time_7b_fp16 = (footprint_7b_fp16 / dram_bw).to(millisecond)
    time_7b_int8 = (footprint_7b_int8 / dram_bw).to(millisecond)
    time_7b_int4 = (footprint_7b_int4 / dram_bw).to(millisecond)
    time_14b_int8 = (footprint_14b_int8 / dram_bw).to(millisecond)

    rate_single_7b_fp16 = (1 / time_7b_fp16).to(hertz)
    rate_single_7b_int8 = (1 / time_7b_int8).to(hertz)
    rate_single_7b_int4 = (1 / time_7b_int4).to(hertz)
    rate_single_14b_int8 = (1 / time_14b_int8).to(hertz)

    rate_chunk_7b_fp16 = rate_single_7b_fp16 * chunk_horizon
    rate_chunk_7b_int8 = rate_single_7b_int8 * chunk_horizon
    rate_chunk_7b_int4 = rate_single_7b_int4 * chunk_horizon
    rate_chunk_14b_int8 = rate_single_14b_int8 * chunk_horizon

    # Safety bounds (N = 3 / lambda)
    hours_asild = (rule_of_three / lambda_asild).to(hour)
    hours_sil3 = (rule_of_three / lambda_sil3).to(hour)
    hours_robotaxi = (rule_of_three / lambda_robotaxi).to(hour)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(intent_hi < chunk_lo, "Intent band sits below chunk band.")
    check(chunk_hi < permission < current_lo, "Permission loop sits between chunk policy and current loop.")
    check(current_hi < switching_lo, "Current loop sits below inverter switching.")
    check(abs(perm_t.magnitude - 1.0) < 1e-9, "1 kHz has 1 ms period.")
    check(abs(time_7b_fp16.magnitude - 100.0) < 1e-3, "14 GB / 140 GB/s is 100 ms.")
    check(abs(time_7b_int8.magnitude - 50.0) < 1e-3, "7 GB / 140 GB/s is 50 ms.")
    check(abs(time_7b_int4.magnitude - 25.0) < 1e-3, "3.5 GB / 140 GB/s is 25 ms.")
    check(abs(hours_asild.magnitude - 3e8) < 1.0, "ASIL D hours: 3e8.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    intent_freq_str = MarkdownStr(f"{fmt(intent_lo.magnitude, precision=0)}–{fmt_frequency(intent_hi, unit=hertz, precision=0)}")
    chunk_freq_str = MarkdownStr(f"{fmt(chunk_lo.magnitude, precision=0)}–{fmt_frequency(chunk_hi, unit=hertz, precision=0)}")
    perm_freq_str = fmt_frequency(permission, unit=ureg.kilohertz, precision=0)
    curr_freq_str = MarkdownStr(f"{fmt(current_lo.magnitude, precision=0)}–{fmt_frequency(current_hi, unit=ureg.kilohertz, precision=0)}")
    sw_freq_str = MarkdownStr(
        f"{fmt(switching_lo.to(ureg.kilohertz).magnitude, precision=0)}–{fmt_frequency(switching_hi, unit=ureg.kilohertz, precision=0)}"
    )

    intent_period_str = MarkdownStr(f"{fmt(intent_t_lo.magnitude, precision=0)}–{fmt(intent_t_hi.magnitude, precision=0)} ms")
    chunk_period_str = MarkdownStr(f"{fmt(chunk_t_lo.magnitude, precision=0)}–{fmt(chunk_t_hi.magnitude, precision=0)} ms")
    perm_period_str = MarkdownStr(f"{fmt(perm_t.magnitude, precision=0)} ms")
    curr_period_str = MarkdownStr(f"{fmt(curr_t_lo.magnitude, precision=0)}–{fmt(curr_t_hi.magnitude, precision=0)} µs")
    sw_period_str = MarkdownStr(f"{fmt(sw_t_lo.magnitude, precision=0)}–{fmt(sw_t_hi.magnitude, precision=0)} µs")

    intent_blind_str = MarkdownStr(f"{fmt(intent_t_lo.magnitude, precision=0)}–{fmt(intent_t_hi.magnitude, precision=0)} mm")
    chunk_blind_str = MarkdownStr(f"{fmt(chunk_t_lo.magnitude, precision=0)}–{fmt(chunk_t_hi.magnitude, precision=0)} mm")
    perm_blind_str = fmt_length(1 * millimeter, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    curr_blind_str = MarkdownStr(f"{fmt(curr_t_lo.magnitude, precision=0)}–{fmt(curr_t_hi.magnitude, precision=0)} µm")
    sw_blind_str = MarkdownStr(f"{fmt(sw_t_lo.magnitude, precision=0)}–{fmt(sw_t_hi.magnitude, precision=0)} µm")

    hum_v_str = MarkdownStr(f"{fmt_velocity(hum_v, unit=_MPS)} ({fmt_velocity(hum_v, unit=kilometer/hour)})")
    rm_v_str = MarkdownStr(f"{fmt_velocity(rm_v, unit=_MPS)} ({fmt_velocity(rm_v, unit=kilometer/hour)})")
    bot_v_str = MarkdownStr(f"{fmt_velocity(bot_v, unit=_MPS)} ({fmt_velocity(bot_v, unit=kilometer/hour)})")
    av_v_str = MarkdownStr(f"{fmt_velocity(av_v, unit=_MPS)} ({fmt_velocity(av_v, unit=kilometer/hour)})")

    hum_a_str = MarkdownStr(
        f"{fmt_acceleration(hum_a, unit=_MPS2)} ({fmt((hum_a/ureg.standard_gravity).to('dimensionless').magnitude, precision=2, suffix=' g')})"
    )
    rm_a_str = MarkdownStr(
        f"{fmt_acceleration(rm_a, unit=_MPS2)} ({fmt((rm_a/ureg.standard_gravity).to('dimensionless').magnitude, precision=2, suffix=' g')})"
    )
    bot_a_str = MarkdownStr(
        f"{fmt_acceleration(bot_a, unit=_MPS2)} ({fmt((bot_a/ureg.standard_gravity).to('dimensionless').magnitude, precision=2, suffix=' g')})"
    )
    av_a_str = MarkdownStr(
        f"{fmt_acceleration(av_a, unit=_MPS2)} ({fmt((av_a/ureg.standard_gravity).to('dimensionless').magnitude, precision=2, suffix=' g')})"
    )

    hum_blind_50_str = fmt_length(hum_blind_50, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    hum_blind_200_str = fmt_length(hum_blind_200, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    hum_stop_200_str = MarkdownStr(
        f"{fmt_length(hum_stop_200, unit=millimeter, precision=0)} ({fmt_percent(hum_share_200, precision=1, style='symbol')})"
    )

    rm_blind_50_str = fmt_length(rm_blind_50, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    rm_blind_200_str = fmt_length(rm_blind_200, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    rm_stop_200_str = MarkdownStr(
        f"{fmt_length(rm_stop_200, unit=millimeter, precision=0)} ({fmt_percent(rm_share_200, precision=1, style='symbol')})"
    )

    bot_blind_50_str = fmt_length(bot_blind_50, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    bot_blind_200_str = fmt_length(bot_blind_200, unit=meter, precision=1)
    bot_stop_200_str = MarkdownStr(f"{fmt_length(bot_stop_200, unit=meter, precision=1)} ({fmt_percent(bot_share_200, precision=1, style='symbol')})")

    av_blind_50_str = fmt_length(av_blind_50, unit=meter, precision=1)
    av_blind_200_str = fmt_length(round(av_blind_200.to(meter).magnitude) * meter, unit=meter, precision=0)
    av_stop_200_str = MarkdownStr(
        f"{fmt_length(round(av_stop_200.to(meter).magnitude, 1) * meter, unit=meter, precision=1)} ({fmt_percent(av_share_200, precision=1, style='symbol')})"
    )

    fp_7b_fp16_str = fmt_memory(footprint_7b_fp16, unit=GB, precision=0)
    fp_7b_int8_str = fmt_memory(footprint_7b_int8, unit=GB, precision=0)
    fp_7b_int4_str = fmt_memory(footprint_7b_int4, unit=GB, precision=1)
    fp_14b_int8_str = fmt_memory(footprint_14b_int8, unit=GB, precision=0)

    t_7b_fp16_str = fmt_latency(time_7b_fp16, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_7b_int8_str = fmt_latency(time_7b_int8, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_7b_int4_str = fmt_latency(time_7b_int4, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_14b_int8_str = fmt_latency(time_14b_int8, unit=millisecond, precision=0)

    rate_s_7b_fp16_str = fmt_frequency(rate_single_7b_fp16, unit=hertz, precision=0)
    rate_s_7b_int8_str = fmt_frequency(rate_single_7b_int8, unit=hertz, precision=0)
    rate_s_7b_int4_str = fmt_frequency(rate_single_7b_int4, unit=hertz, precision=0)
    rate_s_14b_int8_str = fmt_frequency(rate_single_14b_int8, unit=hertz, precision=0)

    rate_c_7b_fp16_str = fmt_frequency(rate_chunk_7b_fp16, unit=hertz, precision=0)
    rate_c_7b_int8_str = fmt_frequency(rate_chunk_7b_int8, unit=hertz, precision=0)
    rate_c_7b_int4_str = fmt_frequency(rate_chunk_7b_int4, unit=hertz, precision=0)
    rate_c_14b_int8_str = fmt_frequency(rate_chunk_14b_int8, unit=hertz, precision=0)
```

Just as Jeff Dean's "Latency Numbers Every Programmer Should Know"[^fn-sys-jeff-dean] shaped distributed systems and classical machine learning systems grounded software performance in memory bandwidth and arithmetic intensity, physical AI systems engineers require a corresponding quantitative intuition spanning computation, kinetics, thermal dissipation, and functional safety. In distributed computing clusters, latency is evaluated across storage tiers, DRAM buses, PCIe links, and InfiniBand network hops to optimize throughput and tail latency. In physical AI, however, software latency is not merely waiting time; it translates directly into irreversible kinetic momentum, uninspected travel distance, and thermodynamic heat accumulation in motor stators and compute silicon.

This section compiles the foundational order-of-magnitude numbers, scaling laws, and engineering rules of thumb that govern cyber-physical machine design. All numbers are single-sourced from `mlsysim`. Memorize the relationships; use the specific numbers as sanity checks.

[^fn-sys-jeff-dean]: **Jeff Dean**\index{Dean, Jeff!latency numbers}: Google Senior Fellow and systems architect. His latency numbers originally presented with Peter Norvig around 2010 established the canonical latency hierarchy across storage, memory, and network tiers [@scott2012latency]. Physical AI extends this hierarchy down into electromechanical actuators, stopping kinematics, and thermal time constants.

::: {#psp-appendix-systems-three-numbers .callout-perspective title="Three physical numbers that matter most"}

* **Kinetic equivalence: $1\text{ ms} = 1\text{ mm}$ (at $1\text{ m/s}$)**: At a nominal robotic speed of $1\text{ m/s}$, every single millisecond of perception, inference, or fieldbus latency translates into exactly $1\text{ mm}$ of blind travel before retarding torque can be applied. At highway velocity ($30\text{ m/s}$), each millisecond is $3\text{ cm}$. In physical systems, software latency is not waiting time; it is physical displacement.
* **Thermal divergence: $\tau_{\text{silicon}} \sim 1\text{ ms}$ vs. $\tau_{\text{stator}} \sim 100\text{ s}$**: Semiconductor junctions heat adiabatically within milliseconds during deep neural network bursts, precipitating voltage droop or thermal throttling before heat spreaders react. In contrast, electromagnetic stator windings heat over tens to hundreds of seconds, tolerating transient overcurrent for aggressive maneuvers but accumulating thermal energy that eventually limits sustained torque.
* **The exposure wall: $N = 3 / \lambda$**: Proving an ultra-low catastrophic failure rate of $10^{-8}/\text{hour}$ (ISO 26262 ASIL D) requires $3 \times 10^8$ failure-free operational hours under the Poisson Rule of Three [@hanley1983nothing]. Statistical empirical testing of learned end-to-end models cannot cross this exposure wall without deterministic runtime permission envelopes and formal safety filters.

:::

### Rate and latency hierarchy across machine levels

Control rates in physical AI rise steeply from the deliberative brain down to the physical body (@tbl-numbers-rate-hierarchy). Deliberative multimodal models (VLAs) operate at human reaction scales ($1\text{--}5\text{ Hz}$). Action chunking models emit future trajectory waypoints at $10\text{--}50\text{ Hz}$. Beneath the proposal boundary, the permission path enforces safety barriers at $1\text{ kHz}$. At the lowest levels, power electronic current loops and PWM switching operate at tens to hundreds of kilohertz to maintain electromagnetic flux and drive torque. For real-time timer schedulability and response-time analysis, see @sec-appendix-systems-timers; for inverter gate switching and dead-time modeling, see @sec-appendix-systems-inverters.

| Machine Level                   | Frequency Band                                   | Cycle Period                                       | Blind Travel at 1 m/s                             | Architectural Mechanism & Bound                                                   |
|:--------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Brain (Deliberation)**        | `{python} PhysicalNumbersToKnow.intent_freq_str` | `{python} PhysicalNumbersToKnow.intent_period_str` | `{python} PhysicalNumbersToKnow.intent_blind_str` | Multimodal VLA reasoning; memory- and compute-bound                               |
| **Brain (Action Chunking)**     | `{python} PhysicalNumbersToKnow.chunk_freq_str`  | `{python} PhysicalNumbersToKnow.chunk_period_str`  | `{python} PhysicalNumbersToKnow.chunk_blind_str`  | Action chunk diffusion/transformer decoding; amortized                            |
| **Nervous System (Permission)** | `{python} PhysicalNumbersToKnow.perm_freq_str`   | `{python} PhysicalNumbersToKnow.perm_period_str`   | `{python} PhysicalNumbersToKnow.perm_blind_str`   | Control barrier certificates, stopping envelopes, lease watchdog                  |
| **Body (Current Loop)**         | `{python} PhysicalNumbersToKnow.curr_freq_str`   | `{python} PhysicalNumbersToKnow.curr_period_str`   | `{python} PhysicalNumbersToKnow.curr_blind_str`   | Field-oriented current control (FOC), torque tracking, stator flux                |
| **Body (Inverter Switching)**   | `{python} PhysicalNumbersToKnow.sw_freq_str`     | `{python} PhysicalNumbersToKnow.sw_period_str`     | `{python} PhysicalNumbersToKnow.sw_blind_str`     | Power MOSFET gate drive, dead-time insertion ($t_{\text{dead}}$), inductive droop |

: **Rate and Latency Hierarchy Across the Five Machine Levels**: Spanning five frequency decades from sub-microsecond MOSFET gate switching up to second-scale foundation model deliberation. Every frequency band imposes a hard cycle period and an uninspected physical travel distance at nominal speed ($1\text{ m/s}$). {#tbl-numbers-rate-hierarchy tbl-colwidths="[18,16,16,18,32]"}

### Kinetic translation and safe stopping envelopes

Total stopping distance $d_{\text{stop}} = v \cdot \tau_{\text{delay}} + v^2 / (2 a_{\text{brake}})$ combines the linear blind travel accrued during computational delay and the quadratic mechanical braking distance (@tbl-numbers-kinematics). As platform speed increases, absolute blind travel expands rapidly, consuming entire clearance margins before deceleration can begin. For multi-axis kinematic chains, jerk-bounded trajectories, and information-age lag derivations, see @sec-appendix-systems-stopping.

| Platform Archetype               | Nominal Velocity $v$                       | Braking Decel $a$                          | Blind Travel ($\tau=50\text{ ms}$)                | Blind Travel ($\tau=200\text{ ms}$)                | Total Stop ($\tau=200\text{ ms}$)                 |
|:---------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------|
| **Humanoid / Quadruped**         | `{python} PhysicalNumbersToKnow.hum_v_str` | `{python} PhysicalNumbersToKnow.hum_a_str` | `{python} PhysicalNumbersToKnow.hum_blind_50_str` | `{python} PhysicalNumbersToKnow.hum_blind_200_str` | `{python} PhysicalNumbersToKnow.hum_stop_200_str` |
| **Warehouse Mobile Manipulator** | `{python} PhysicalNumbersToKnow.rm_v_str`  | `{python} PhysicalNumbersToKnow.rm_a_str`  | `{python} PhysicalNumbersToKnow.rm_blind_50_str`  | `{python} PhysicalNumbersToKnow.rm_blind_200_str`  | `{python} PhysicalNumbersToKnow.rm_stop_200_str`  |
| **Urban Delivery Robot**         | `{python} PhysicalNumbersToKnow.bot_v_str` | `{python} PhysicalNumbersToKnow.bot_a_str` | `{python} PhysicalNumbersToKnow.bot_blind_50_str` | `{python} PhysicalNumbersToKnow.bot_blind_200_str` | `{python} PhysicalNumbersToKnow.bot_stop_200_str` |
| **Autonomous Vehicle (Highway)** | `{python} PhysicalNumbersToKnow.av_v_str`  | `{python} PhysicalNumbersToKnow.av_a_str`  | `{python} PhysicalNumbersToKnow.av_blind_50_str`  | `{python} PhysicalNumbersToKnow.av_blind_200_str`  | `{python} PhysicalNumbersToKnow.av_stop_200_str`  |

: **Kinetic Translation Across Platform Archetypes**: Pre-brake delay converts into unrecoverable physical travel before braking force begins. Stopping distance $d_{\text{stop}} = v \cdot \tau_{\text{delay}} + v^2 / (2 a_{\text{brake}})$ combines linear blind travel and quadratic braking distance. {#tbl-numbers-kinematics tbl-colwidths="[20,16,16,16,16,16]"}

### Edge memory bandwidth and action chunk amortization

Large multimodal foundation models on edge system-on-chip (SoC) architectures are memory-bandwidth bound during autoregressive generation (@tbl-numbers-edge-compute). Streaming a 7-billion-parameter model over a sustained $140\text{ GB/s}$ LPDDR5 interface limits single-step generation to $10\text{--}20\text{ Hz}$. Predicting action chunks of length $H=16$ amortizes the weight streaming transfer over multiple future control steps, lifting effective control bandwidth into the hundreds of hertz. For DRAM bank organization, conflict penalties, and interconnect arbitration under concurrent direct memory access (DMA) traffic, see @sec-appendix-systems-dram.

### Thermal time constants across compute and electromechanics

Thermal dissipation follows an exponential relaxation $T(t) = T_{\text{amb}} + \Delta T_{\max} (1 - e^{-t/\tau_{\text{th}}})$ with time constants spanning five orders of magnitude (@tbl-numbers-thermal). Silicon junctions overheat within milliseconds during computational bursts, demanding microsecond-scale DVFS and PDN droop management. In contrast, electromagnetic stator windings heat over minutes, allowing transient torque overdrive if bounded by an $I^2 t$ thermal watchdog. For first-order thermal differential equations and stator winding degradation limits, see @sec-appendix-systems-actuators; for regenerative energy absorption on DC power buses, see @sec-appendix-systems-power.

| Subsystem Component         | Physical Mechanism                       | Thermal Time Constant $\tau_{\text{th}}$ | Critical Failure Mode                                     | Safety Mitigation                            |
|:----------------------------|:-----------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------|
| **Silicon Junction (Die)**  | Transistor channel self-heating          | 1–10 ms                                  | Gate delay stretch, brownout, thermal trip                | Rapid frequency throttling, PDN decoupling   |
| **SoC Heat Sink / Package** | Convective heat spreader dissipation     | 10–60 s                                  | Package thermal saturation, sustained throttling          | Active fan modulation, workload migration    |
| **Motor Stator Windings**   | Copper resistive Joule heating ($I^2 R$) | 30–180 s                                 | Insulation breakdown (Class H $180^\circ\text{C}$), short | $I^2 t$ thermal protection, current derating |
| **Motor Frame / Housing**   | Bulk metallic casing heat conduction     | 10–30 min                                | Structural deformation, bearing grease loss               | Natural convection, passive cooling fins     |
| **Traction Battery Pack**   | Electrochemical cell internal resistance | 5–20 min                                 | Thermal runaway ($> 60^\circ\text{C}$), fire              | Liquid cooling loop, charge/discharge cutoff |

: **Thermal Time Constants Across Compute and Electromechanical Subsystems**: Thermal inertia spans five orders of magnitude. Adiabatic heating in semiconductor junctions causes rapid thermal throttling within milliseconds, while copper motor windings integrate electrical energy over tens to hundreds of seconds. {#tbl-numbers-thermal tbl-colwidths="[20,18,16,22,24]"}

### Statistical safety bounds and exposure walls

Under the Poisson Rule of Three [@hanley1983nothing], demonstrating that a physical system achieves a catastrophic failure rate target $\lambda$ with $95\text{ percent}$ confidence without observing a single failure requires testing for $N = 3 / \lambda$ operational hours (@tbl-numbers-safety). Meeting the ultra-dependable thresholds demanded by automotive functional safety (ISO 26262 ASIL D, $\lambda < 10^{-8}/\text{hour}$ [@iso26262]) requires 300 million failure-free hours—a scale that renders end-to-end black-box statistical validation mathematically impossible without deterministic runtime permission envelopes. For proposal and manifest wire formats supporting runtime safety contracts, see @sec-appendix-systems-wire-formats.

| Safety Standard / Regime       | Target Failure Rate $\lambda$ | Equivalent FIT ($10^{-9}/\text{h}$) | Required 0-Failure Hours ($N=3/\lambda$)              | Engineering Implication                                                        |
|:-------------------------------|:------------------------------|:------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **ISO 26262 ASIL D**           | $< 10^{-8}/\text{hour}$       | $< 10\text{ FIT}$                   | $300,000,000\text{ hours}$ ($3 \times 10^8\text{ h}$) | Empirically untestable by fleet testing alone; requires formal safety barriers |
| **IEC 61508 SIL 3 / PL e**     | $< 10^{-7}/\text{hour}$       | $< 100\text{ FIT}$                  | $30,000,000\text{ hours}$ ($3 \times 10^7\text{ h}$)  | Dual-channel lockstep hardware, diverse software monitoring                    |
| **Commercial Robotaxi Target** | $< 10^{-6}/\text{hour}$       | $< 1,000\text{ FIT}$                | $3,000,000\text{ hours}$ ($3 \times 10^6\text{ h}$)   | Human driver baseline equivalence ($1$ fatality per $10^8\text{ miles}$)       |
| **Industrial Cobot (PL d)**    | $< 10^{-6}/\text{hour}$       | $< 1,000\text{ FIT}$                | $3,000,000\text{ hours}$ ($3 \times 10^6\text{ h}$)   | Force and power limiting, speed-and-separation monitoring                      |

: **Functional Safety Standards and Statistical Testing Exposure Walls**: Required failure-free operating hours to establish safety targets at $95\text{ percent}$ confidence via the Rule of Three ($N = 3 / \lambda$). Purely statistical end-to-end testing cannot prove catastrophic safety without deterministic runtime guarantees. {#tbl-numbers-safety tbl-colwidths="[20,16,18,22,24]"}

### Fieldbus latencies, jitter, and determinism

Communication buses exhibit sharp divides in latency and jitter (@tbl-numbers-buses). Whereas distributed cluster fabrics (such as RoCEv2 or InfiniBand) prioritize aggregate bandwidth using credit-based flow control and statistical multiplexing, onboard physical AI buses must guarantee bounded delivery times. Industrial fieldbuses like EtherCAT achieve sub-microsecond jitter via dedicated hardware cut-through processing. In contrast, non-deterministic arbitration and shared wireless channels introduce tail latencies that exceed the reaction deadlines of high-speed electromechanical machines. For IEEE 1588 PTP hardware timestamping bounds, see @sec-appendix-systems-ptp; for CAN-FD priority arbitration and EtherCAT cycle budgets, see @sec-appendix-systems-fieldbus.

## Real-Time Timers, Watchdogs, and Schedulability {#sec-appendix-systems-timers}

In distributed machine learning clusters, scheduling frameworks such as the Linux Completely Fair Scheduler (CFS), Slurm, or Kubernetes gang schedulers optimize for aggregate throughput, work-conserving resource utilization, and average tail latency (p99 request response). When a GPU worker or inference server stalls for 50 milliseconds due to a minor page fault, garbage collection sweep, or CPU frequency scaling transition, the cluster merely registers an ephemeral latency spike.

In physical AI systems, however, computation is directly coupled to physical momentum and kinetic energy. An autonomous robot traveling at speed or manipulating heavy loads cannot tolerate unbounded execution delays: an actuator command delivered 10 milliseconds late is not merely degraded—it is computationally incorrect and potentially catastrophic. Real-time embedded systems are not an exercise in obscure microcontroller firmware hacking, but the deterministic operating system infrastructure that bridges high-latency, variable-execution AI accelerators with physical actuators. This infrastructure provides mathematically verifiable bounds on worst-case execution time, preemption latency, resource contention, and fail-safe hardware interlocks.

### Real-time task schedulability under rate-monotonic and earliest-deadline-first scheduling

In contrast to general-purpose Linux time-sharing, real-time operating systems schedule tasks based on deterministic timing contracts rather than dynamic heuristics. A periodic real-time task $\tau_i$ is characterized by its worst-case execution time (WCET) $C_i$, relative deadline $D_i$, and period $T_i$.\index{Real-time systems!worst-case execution time}\index{Rate-Monotonic Scheduling!utilization bound}\index{Earliest Deadline First!dynamic scheduling} When multiple real-time tasks share a single core, schedulability depends on the priority assignment discipline:

**Rate-Monotonic Scheduling (RMS).** Fixed-priority preemptive scheduling where priority is assigned inversely proportional to task period ($T_i < T_j \implies \text{priority}(\tau_i) > \text{priority}(\tau_j)$) [@liu1973scheduling]. For a set of $n$ independent periodic tasks with implicit deadlines ($D_i = T_i$), a sufficient condition for schedulability is the Liu and Layland utilization bound:
$$ U = \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{C_i}{T_i} \le n \left( 2^{1/n} - 1 \right) $$
As $n \to \infty$, the bound converges monotonically to $\lim_{n \to \infty} n(2^{1/n}-1) = \ln 2 \approx 0.693$ (69.3 percent). If total processor utilization does not exceed 69.3 percent, the task set is guaranteed to meet all deadlines under RMS. When task periods form a harmonic set—where every period is an exact integer multiple of every shorter period—the utilization bound rises to 100 percent.

**Response Time Analysis (RTA).** When processor utilization exceeds the conservative Liu and Layland bound ($U > \ln 2$), or when relative deadlines are constrained ($D_i \le T_i$), exact schedulability requires evaluating the worst-case **response time** $R_i$ [@liu1973scheduling; @kopetz2011real]:
$$ R_i = C_i + B_i + I_i \le D_i $$
where $B_i$ is the maximum blocking duration induced by lower-priority tasks holding shared resources, and $I_i$ is the interference from higher-priority tasks. The response time is computed via the fixed-point recurrence:
$$ R_i^{(k+1)} = C_i + B_i + \sum_{j \in hp(i)} \left\lceil \frac{R_i^{(k)}}{T_j} \right\rceil C_j $$
starting with $R_i^{(0)} = C_i + B_i$ and iterating until $R_i^{(k+1)} = R_i^{(k)} \le D_i$ (establishing schedulability) or $R_i^{(k+1)} > D_i$ (signaling deadline violation). See @sec-nervous-schedulability-analysis and @sec-nervous-rta-variance for the role of response time variance in the nervous system.

**Earliest Deadline First (EDF).** In dynamic-priority systems, EDF assigns highest priority to the active task with the closest absolute deadline $d_{i,k} = r_{i,k} + D_i$. On a single-core preemptive processor, EDF is optimal: if a task set is schedulable by any scheduling algorithm, it is schedulable by EDF [@liu1973scheduling]. For periodic tasks with $D_i = T_i$, EDF guarantees schedulability if and only if:
$$ \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{C_i}{T_i} \le 1 $$
achieving 100 percent theoretical utilization without requiring harmonic periods. When relative deadlines are strictly less than periods ($D_i < T_i$), schedulability requires the processor demand criterion over the Demand Bound Function (DBF):
$$ \text{dbf}(t) = \sum_{i=1}^n \max\left( 0, \left\lfloor \frac{t - D_i}{T_i} \right\rfloor + 1 \right) C_i \le t, \quad \forall t \ge 0 $$
evaluating whether cumulative execution demand exceeds available physical time across all time intervals $t$.

**Priority Inversion and Resource Sharing.** In standard multi-threaded Linux, mutual exclusion primitives (such as futex-backed mutexes) assume threads will eventually yield the processor. When real-time tasks share data structures (such as seqlock mailboxes or actuator command queues) protected by naive mutual exclusion, they suffer from **unbounded priority inversion** [@sha1990priority; @reeves1997pathfinder]. A low-priority task $\tau_L$ acquires a lock; a high-priority task $\tau_H$ becomes ready and blocks waiting for the lock; intermediate-priority tasks $\tau_M$ that do not need the lock preempt $\tau_L$, delaying $\tau_H$ for an arbitrary duration.

To bound blocking time $B_i$ in the RTA recurrence, real-time operating systems employ formal synchronization protocols:

1. **Priority Inheritance Protocol (PIP)**: When $\tau_H$ blocks on a lock held by $\tau_L$, the operating system temporarily elevates $\tau_L$'s active priority to $\tau_H$'s priority, preventing preemption by $\tau_M$. Under `PREEMPT_RT` Linux, standard in-kernel spinlocks are converted to sleeping `rt_mutex` locks that enforce PIP automatically, while user-space threads configure `PTHREAD_PRIO_INHERIT`. While PIP eliminates unbounded inversion, it permits transitive blocking chains and potential deadlock.
2. **Priority Ceiling Protocol (PCP)**: Each lock is assigned a static priority ceiling equal to the highest priority of any task that may lock it. A task $\tau_i$ can lock a resource only if its priority is strictly higher than the priority ceilings of all locks currently held by other tasks. PCP prevents mutual-exclusion deadlocks and guarantees that a task is blocked at most once by at most one lower-priority critical section [@sha1990priority]:
$$ B_i = \max_{k \in lp(i), s \in cs(k)} C_{k,s} $$
where $lp(i)$ is the set of tasks with priority lower than $\tau_i$, and $cs(k)$ is the set of critical sections executed by task $\tau_k$ with a priority ceiling at or above the priority of $\tau_i$.

### Worst-case execution time analysis for physical ML pipelines

In classical embedded systems, the worst-case execution time $C_i$ is determined via Static Timing Analysis (STA) [@hennessy2019computer]. STA parses binary machine instructions, constructs a Control Flow Graph (CFG), and solves an Integer Linear Program via the Implicit Path Enumeration Technique (IPET) using cycle-accurate microarchitectural models of processor pipelines, branch predictors, and cache sets.

In physical AI systems, evaluating $C_i$ for learned vision-language-action (VLA) and diffusion policies presents distinct architectural challenges:\index{Physical AI!WCET analysis}\index{Extreme Value Theory!execution time tail bounds}

1. **Microarchitectural opacity**: Modern neural accelerators (GPUs, NPUs, Tensor Processing Unit (TPU) hardware) feature multi-level shared caches, dynamic frequency scaling (DVFS), out-of-order warp schedulers, and memory crossbar contention that preclude cycle-accurate static modeling.
2. **Algorithmic execution variance**: Learned pipelines exhibit dynamic execution paths, including adaptive denoising loops in diffusion models, variable sequence lengths in autoregressive decoders, and data-dependent sparse attention kernels.
3. **Software runtime overhead**: Deep learning runtimes (e.g., TensorRT, Open Neural Network Exchange (ONNX) Runtime) introduce non-deterministic host-to-device kernel launch queueing, unified memory migration, and internal memory allocation locks.

To establish bounded execution times for neural policies that cross the proposal boundary, physical AI systems enforce deterministic execution contracts and hybrid measurement bounds:

* **Static shape contracts**: Action chunk horizons ($H$), token context lengths, and sensor input tensors are locked to fixed maximum dimensions. Dynamic input padding replaces variable-length tensors, ensuring constant compute graph geometry and eliminating dynamic kernel recompilation.
* **Zero runtime allocation**: All execution buffers, KV caches, scratchpad memory, and DMA descriptors are preallocated during initialization. Dynamic memory calls (`malloc`, `cudaMalloc`, `free`) are strictly forbidden on cyclic control paths.
* **Deterministic kernel dispatch**: Denoising iterations are fixed (e.g., exactly 4 or 8 Euler steps) rather than dynamically terminated via convergence thresholds. Furthermore, capturing deep learning pipelines into static execution graphs (such as CUDA Graphs) eliminates host-side kernel launch queueing and driver lock contention by submitting the entire multi-kernel directed acyclic graph (DAG) as a single hardware command.
* **Extreme Value Theory (EVT) tail bounds**: Because finite empirical profiling cannot expose the true maximum execution time under worst-case hardware interference, engineers apply Extreme Value Theory [@coles2001introduction]. Profiling execution times across diverse operational workloads yields a sample distribution whose upper tail is modeled via a Generalized Extreme Value (GEV) distribution:
$$ F(x) = \exp\left( -\left[ 1 + \xi \left( \frac{x - \mu}{\sigma} \right) \right]^{-1/\xi} \right) $$
where $\mu$ is the location, $\sigma > 0$ the scale, and $\xi$ the shape parameter. The certified WCET bound $C_{\text{WCET}}(\epsilon)$ is computed for an acceptable target exceedance probability $\epsilon$ (such as $10^{-6}$ or $10^{-8}$ per invocation):
$$ C_{\text{WCET}}(\epsilon) = \mu - \frac{\sigma}{\xi} \left[ 1 - (-\ln(1 - \epsilon))^{-\xi} \right] $$
This statistical ceiling anchors the loaded execution bounds declared in the placement record (@sec-placement-hardware-allocation, @sec-appendix-systems-wire-placement) and protects the response-time budget of downstream safety enforcers.

### Operating-system determinism through interrupt handling and memory locking

On heterogeneous robotics SoCs, the nervous system and safety monitors execute under real-time operating systems (RTOS) or real-time Linux kernels (such as Linux patched with `PREEMPT_RT`).\index{Real-time operating system!interrupt latency}\index{Memory locking!mlockall page fault elimination}\index{Real-time Linux!kernel mechanics} In standard general-purpose Linux kernels, execution threads in interrupt contexts or kernel critical sections holding non-preemptible spinlocks can stall user-space tasks indefinitely. In physical AI pipelines where control loops govern physical momentum, operating-system determinism requires eliminating non-preemptible kernel sections, bounding interrupt preemption latency, and locking virtual memory.

**PREEMPT_RT Kernel Architecture.** Mainline Linux achieves high throughput by disabling kernel preemption during spinlock acquisition (`preempt_disable()`), deferring interrupts via softirqs, and batching task scheduling. When an unprivileged machine learning process or device driver holds an in-kernel spinlock, a high-priority 1 kHz real-time safety task cannot preempt the CPU, even if its timer has expired. The `PREEMPT_RT` patch transforms Linux into a hard real-time operating system via three structural changes:

1. *Sleeping Spinlocks (`rt_mutex`)*: Standard kernel spinlocks (`spinlock_t` and `rwlock_t`) are converted to sleeping mutexes with Priority Inheritance Protocol (PIP) support. When a real-time thread preempts a lower-priority task holding an `rt_mutex`, the lower-priority task sleeps rather than spinning with preemption disabled, and its priority is elevated to prevent unbounded priority inversion. Critical sections that must execute with local CPU interrupts disabled are strictly minimized to low-level hardware access.
2. *Forced Interrupt Threading*: Hardware interrupt service routines (ISRs) are split into minimal top-half handlers and prioritized kernel threads (`irq/<irq>-<name>`) scheduled under the real-time `SCHED_FIFO` policy.
3. *High-Resolution Timers (`hrtimers`)*: Traditional Linux timer ticks execute at coarse periodic jiffies ($1\text{ ms}$ or $4\text{ ms}$ granularity), introducing substantial quantization error and timer slack. `PREEMPT_RT` binds the timer subsystem to hardware per-CPU clock event devices (such as the ARM Generic Timer or x86 Local APIC), enabling sub-microsecond timer resolution. Real-time cyclic threads invoke `clock_nanosleep(CLOCK_MONOTONIC, TIMER_ABSTIME, &next_period, NULL)` using absolute monotonic deadlines, eliminating phase jitter and cumulative drift across successive control cycles.

**Interrupt Handling Latency and Top-Half/Bottom-Half Partitioning.** When an external hardware peripheral (such as an IMU, joint encoder counter, or fieldbus controller) asserts an interrupt request (IRQ), the processor halts user execution, saves register context, and vectors to the hardware ISR. The worst-case interrupt latency $t_{\text{irq,lat}}$ before a real-time user-space control thread begins execution is bounded by:
$$ t_{\text{irq,lat}} = t_{\text{irq\_disabled,max}} + t_{\text{hw\_pipe}} + t_{\text{context\_save}} + \sum_{j \in hp(\text{irq})} t_{\text{ISR},j} $$
where $t_{\text{irq\_disabled,max}}$ is the longest duration during which CPU interrupts were disabled across the kernel, $t_{\text{hw\_pipe}}$ is the processor pipeline flush delay, $t_{\text{context\_save}}$ is the hardware register preservation time, and $\sum t_{\text{ISR},j}$ represents the execution duration of higher-priority ISRs.

To prevent high-bandwidth sensor streams (such as GigE Vision cameras or 3D lidars streaming gigabits of packet traffic) from generating an *interrupt storm* that starves the 1 kHz permission path, real-time architectures strictly enforce top-half and bottom-half partitioning:

* **Top-half (Hardware ISR)**: Executes in hard-interrupt context with CPU interrupts masked. It executes the absolute minimum hardware operations—reading the peripheral interrupt status register, clearing the physical interrupt line, latching high-resolution hardware counter timestamps, and waking the associated threaded IRQ. Execution time is strictly bounded to sub-microsecond intervals.
* **Bottom-half (Threaded IRQ)**: In `PREEMPT_RT` and RTOS environments, complex packet deserialization, frame CRC verification, and data copies are deferred to dedicated kernel threads (`irq/<irq>-<name>`). By configuring these threaded IRQs under `SCHED_FIFO` with priorities lower than the 1 kHz safety monitor (e.g., setting camera IRQ threads to priority 50 and the motor permission thread to priority 90), the system guarantees that high-rate perception ingress can never preempt the deterministic control loop.

**Memory Locking and Page Fault Elimination.** Virtual memory subsystems rely on demand paging: when a process accesses an unmapped virtual address, the CPU raises an architectural page fault exception (`#PF`), suspending execution while the kernel page-table handler allocates a physical page frame, updates translation lookaside buffer (TLB) entries, and zeroes the memory (a *minor page fault*, requiring $10\text{--}50\,\mu\text{s}$). If the requested page was swapped to secondary flash storage, the thread blocks on disk I/O (a *major page fault*, requiring $10\text{--}50\text{ ms}$). A single page fault on a cyclic control path instantly violates the 1 ms permission deadline.

To achieve hard real-time determinism in user space, real-time control processes must implement a four-part memory locking and initialization protocol:

```c
// Real-time process memory initialization
#include <sys/mman.h>
#include <malloc.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

void configure_realtime_memory(size_t stack_size) {
    // 1. Lock all current and future mapped address pages into physical RAM
    if (mlockall(MCL_CURRENT | MCL_FUTURE) != 0) {
        perror("mlockall failed");
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }

    // 2. Disable dynamic glibc heap trimming and anonymous mmap growth
    mallopt(M_TRIM_THRESHOLD, -1);
    mallopt(M_MMAP_MAX, 0);

    // 3. Prefault the thread execution stack to its declared maximum depth
    volatile char stack_buffer[stack_size];
    for (size_t i = 0; i < stack_size; i += 4096) {
        stack_buffer[i] = 0; // Force physical page allocation and TLB entry
    }
}
```

Beyond address space locking and stack prefaulting, the cyclic 1 kHz control loop operates under a strict **zero dynamic allocation invariant**. Dynamic memory allocators (`malloc`, `free`, C++ `new`, `delete`) utilize global arena mutexes, manage complex bucket free-lists, and suffer from heap fragmentation that induces non-deterministic latency. All message structures, matrix workspace buffers, trajectory buffers, and seqlock mailbox slots must be statically allocated at startup or drawn from fixed-size, lock-free memory pools.

### Hardware watchdogs and fault response

In distributed computing clusters, node liveness and consensus are managed via software heartbeats and distributed leases (such as Raft heartbeats, ZooKeeper leases, or Kubernetes node probes) operating over second-scale intervals. If a worker node crashes, the cluster orchestrator reschedules containers onto alternative nodes.

In physical AI systems, an autonomous machine traveling through physical space cannot wait seconds for a software orchestrator. If the GPU driver deadlocks, memory bus crossbars stall, or a kernel panic freezes the operating system, physical momentum continues unchecked. To detect a missed execution checkpoint, an embedded design uses a **hardware watchdog timer**.\index{Watchdog timer!hardware downcounter}\index{Watchdog timer!windowed watchdog}\index{Watchdog timer!token-passing liveness} Its clock and response path must be independent of the monitored processor; an independent crystal oscillator or low-speed internal oscillator (`LSI`) completely decoupled from the main system phase-locked loop (PLL) is required.

**Hardware Down-Counters and Windowed Servicing.** The hardware watchdog timer comprises an autonomous down-counter register $W(t)$ clocked at frequency $f_{\text{wdg}}$. At system initialization, the register is loaded with a threshold value $W_{\text{init}}$. Software execution threads must periodically refresh (or "kick") the register before the count decrements to zero:
$$ W(t_k) = W_{\text{init}} $$
In safety-critical systems, simple down-counters are vulnerable to runaway execution bugs: if a corrupted control loop enters an infinite spin-loop that happens to execute the watchdog refresh instruction, the watchdog is continually fed despite the control failure. To prevent this, robust physical AI architectures employ a **Windowed Watchdog Timer (WWDG)**. A windowed watchdog defines both an upper bound $W_{\text{upper}}$ and a lower bound $W_{\text{lower}}$. The software refresh is valid only within the admissible time window:
$$ W_{\text{lower}} \le W(t_k) \le W_{\text{upper}} $$
If software attempts to refresh the watchdog too early ($W(t_k) > W_{\text{upper}}$)—indicating an abnormal loop short-circuit—or fails to refresh before underflow ($W(t_k) < W_{\text{lower}}$), the hardware watchdog controller trips immediately.

**Multi-Stage Token-Passing Liveness Checkpoints.** Feeding the watchdog directly from a periodic timer interrupt is an unsafe anti-pattern, because the timer interrupt may continue firing even if the primary motion planning and safety monitor threads are deadlocked. To guarantee that the watchdog monitors true algorithmic progression, control software implements **token-passing checkpointing**:

1. At the beginning of the 1 kHz tick, an execution token $T_0$ is generated.
2. Stage 1 (Sensor Ingress): Validates camera, IMU, and joint telemetry timestamps, updating the token: $T_1 = \text{hash}(T_0, \text{sensor\_valid})$.
3. Stage 2 (State Estimation & Tracking): Computes joint tracking errors, updating $T_2 = \text{hash}(T_1, \text{tracking\_valid})$.
4. Stage 3 (Permission Enforcer): Validates Control Barrier Functions and stopping distance envelopes, computing $T_3 = \text{hash}(T_2, \text{enforce\_valid})$.
5. Stage 4 (Actuator Dispatch): Transmits admitted setpoints across the fieldbus, computing $T_{\text{final}} = \text{hash}(T_3, \text{dispatch\_valid})$.

Only if $T_{\text{final}}$ matches the precomputed valid signature will the watchdog refresh routine write to the memory-mapped watchdog service register.

**Hardware Fail-Safe Interlocks and Safe Torque Off.** If the software misses its refresh window, the hardware down-counter reaches zero, asserting a non-maskable interrupt (NMI) and triggering an autonomous hardware trip. Crucially, the watchdog's physical trip line is hardwired independently of the monitored microcontroller:

* It drives an external high-reliability optocoupler or solid-state safety relay.
* The relay directly breaks the bias supply to the inverter gate drivers, asserting **Safe Torque Off (STO)**.
* Actuator power stages enter a high-impedance state within microseconds ($< 2.0\,\mu\text{s}$), cutting stator electromagnetic torque at the silicon level regardless of whether the application CPU is halted, in an infinite loop, or experiencing a kernel panic.[^fn-sys-watchdog-reset]

[^fn-sys-watchdog-reset]: **Hardware Watchdog Down-Counters**\index{Watchdog timer!hardware downcounter}: A configured watchdog expires when its expected service does not occur. Its oscillator, timeout, output wiring, and plant response differ by device. Feeding it merely from an unrelated interrupt does not prove that the monitored control computation progressed; a firmware-fed reset also need not signal a drive. See the [Linux watchdog API](https://docs.kernel.org/watchdog/watchdog-api.html) for reset behavior and @sec-enforcement-fallback-ladder for stop selection.

## Inverter Timers and Power Electronics Gate Drive {#sec-appendix-systems-inverters}

In machine learning control frameworks (such as reinforcement learning policies, imitation learning, or model predictive control pipelines), actuator actions are formulated as continuous numerical setpoints—such as commanded joint torques $\boldsymbol{\tau}^*$ or angular velocities $\dot{\mathbf{q}}^*$. In physical realization, however, torque is generated by synthesizing rotating electromagnetic stator flux through high-frequency switching of power semiconductor bridges (typically at $20\text{ kHz}$ to $100\text{ kHz}$). Actuator motor drives employ three-phase half-bridge inverters to convert DC bus voltage into alternating stator currents.

### Microcontroller timer dead-time insertion

Bridging the digital software domain with physical power silicon requires strict microarchitectural timing interlocks. Each inverter phase comprises a half-bridge with a high-side power MOSFET (or GaN FET / IGBT) and a low-side power MOSFET connected across the DC supply rail $V_{\text{bus}}$. Microcontroller timer peripherals generate complementary pulse-width-modulated (PWM) drive signals with hardware-enforced **dead-time insertion** $t_{\text{dead}}$:\index{Pulse-width modulation!dead-time insertion}\index{Inverter!shoot-through protection}\index{Inverter!dead-time distortion}
$$ t_{\text{dead}} \ge t_{\text{off, max}} + t_{\text{prop, skew}} - t_{\text{on, min}} + t_{\text{margin}} $$
where $t_{\text{off, max}}$ is the maximum turn-off delay of the power switch, $t_{\text{on, min}}$ is the minimum turn-on delay, $t_{\text{prop, skew}}$ is the propagation delay mismatch across isolated gate drivers, and $t_{\text{margin}}$ is an engineering safety buffer.[^fn-sys-pwm-deadtime]

**Gate Charge Dynamics and Asymmetric Switching.** A power MOSFET or GaN FET switch possesses input gate capacitance $C_{\text{iss}} = C_{\text{gs}} + C_{\text{gd}}$, where $C_{\text{gd}}$ is the non-linear reverse transfer (Miller) capacitance. During switching, the gate driver must source or sink peak current $I_{\text{g,peak}} \approx (V_{\text{drive}} - V_{\text{plateau}}) / R_{\text{g,ext}}$. During turn-off, the gate voltage dwells at the Miller plateau while drain-to-source voltage rises across the bus, extending the turn-off duration significantly beyond the turn-on time ($t_{\text{off}} > t_{\text{on}}$).

**Shoot-Through Prevention.** If dead time is insufficient or eliminated by software error, both high-side and low-side switches conduct simultaneously. This creates a low-impedance path directly bridging the DC rail to ground:
$$ I_{\text{shoot-through}} = \frac{V_{\text{bus}}}{2 R_{\text{ds(on)}} + R_{\text{trace}}} $$
On a $48\text{ V}$ or $400\text{ V}$ bus with $R_{\text{ds(on)}} = 5\text{ m}\Omega$, short-circuit current surges to hundreds or thousands of amperes within nanoseconds, instantly exceeding silicon thermal safe operating area (SOA) limits and vaporizing bond wires. Dedicated microcontroller timer peripherals (such as STM32 Advanced-control timers TIM1/TIM8 or TI C2000 ePWM modules) feature hardware Dead-Time Generators (DTG). The DTG intercepts complementary PWM outputs and locks rising edges behind hardware counters, rendering shoot-through physically impossible regardless of user-space firmware state.

**Dead-Time Voltage Distortion and Torque Ripple.** While necessary for silicon survival, dead time introduces non-linear voltage distortion into stator windings. During the dead-time interval $t_{\text{dead}}$, both active MOSFET gates are closed, and phase current $I_{\text{phase}}$ is forced to freewheel through antiparallel body diodes. The sign of the phase current determines whether the inverter phase node clamps to $V_{\text{bus}}$ or ground, producing an average phase voltage error:
$$ \Delta V_{\text{phase}} = -\operatorname{sgn}(I_{\text{phase}}) \cdot \frac{t_{\text{dead}}}{T_{\text{pwm}}} V_{\text{bus}} $$
In three-phase synchronous machines, this square-wave error injects 5th and 7th harmonic voltages in the stationary $\alpha\beta$ frame, which transform into a **6th harmonic torque ripple** in the rotor synchronous $dq$ reference frame ($f_{\text{ripple}} = 6 f_e$). Left uncompensated by low-level Field-Oriented Control (FOC) current loops, this hardware-induced torque ripple produces high-frequency torque chatter that degrades high-level trajectory precision.

[^fn-sys-pwm-deadtime]: **Inverter Dead-Time Insertion**\index{Pulse-width modulation!dead-time insertion}: Timer dead time is selected from switch and driver timing over temperature and load, then verified with the actual gate waveforms. An overlap can create a damaging bus short; a numeric current or fuse outcome requires the circuit impedance and protection response.

## Inductive Voltage Droop and Gate Delay Stretch {#sec-appendix-systems-droop}

In data center machine learning clusters, power delivery networks (PDNs) are supported by massive rack-level voltage regulator modules (VRMs) and extensive decoupling capacitor planes. On embedded Physical AI compute platforms, deep learning accelerators (such as tensor cores and systolic array matrix engines) share tightly constrained power rails with CPU cores and real-time safety microcontrollers. When a deep neural network transitions from idle to full execution, current draw increases by tens of amperes within nanoseconds.

### Power delivery network impedance and rail droop

Every power delivery network (PDN) exhibits finite parasitic loop inductance $L_{\text{PDN}}$ and equivalent series resistance $R_{\text{PDN}}$ across PCB traces, package BGA balls, and bond wires. When an accelerator initiates a burst of dense general matrix multiplication (GEMM) operations, current draw jumps by $\Delta I$ with nanosecond rise time $t_r$, yielding current slew rates $dI/dt = \Delta I / t_r \sim 10^8\text{--}10^9\text{ A/s}$. Faraday's law of induction dictates an instantaneous voltage collapse $\Delta V_{\text{droop}}$ across the supply rail:\index{Inductive voltage droop!power delivery network}\index{Power delivery network!target impedance}\index{Decoupling capacitors!multi-tier hierarchy}
$$ \Delta V_{\text{droop}} = L_{\text{PDN}} \frac{dI}{dt} + \Delta I \cdot R_{\text{PDN}} $$

**PDN Target Impedance.** To prevent rail excursions from exceeding allowable voltage tolerances $\pm \Delta V_{\max} = V_{\text{nom}} \times \delta_{\text{tol}}$ (typically $\pm 5\%$, or $45\text{ mV}$ on a $0.9\text{ V}$ digital core rail), the power delivery network must maintain an impedance profile strictly below the **target impedance** $Z_{\text{target}}$ across the entire operational frequency band:
$$ Z_{\text{target}} = \frac{V_{\text{nom}} \cdot \delta_{\text{tol}}}{\Delta I_{\max}} $$
For a $0.9\text{ V}$ accelerator drawing a $50\text{ A}$ step transient with $5\%$ allowable ripple, $Z_{\text{target}} = 45\text{ mV} / 50\text{ A} = 0.90\text{ m}\Omega$ from DC up to gigahertz frequencies.

**Multi-Tier Decoupling Hierarchy.** Switched-mode power supplies (VRMs) have limited feedback control loop bandwidth ($100\text{ kHz}$ to $1\text{ MHz}$) and cannot supply charge during nanosecond current transitions. Energy must be buffered across a multi-tier decoupling capacitor hierarchy:

1. *On-Die Decoupling*: Deep trench and metal-insulator-metal (MIM) capacitors fabricated directly on the silicon die ($C_{\text{die}} \sim 10\text{--}100\text{ nF}$, parasitic loop inductance $< 10\text{ pH}$, response time $< 0.5\text{ ns}$) supply charge during the initial clock cycles.
2. *Package Decoupling*: Land-side capacitors (LSC) mounted under the BGA package ($C_{\text{pkg}} \sim 1\text{--}10\,\mu\text{F}$, loop inductance $\sim 50\text{--}200\text{ pH}$, response time $1\text{--}5\text{ ns}$).
3. *Board-Level High-Frequency MLCCs*: Low-ESL surface-mount multi-layer ceramic capacitors (0201/0402 case sizes, $C \sim 0.1\text{--}10\,\mu\text{F}$, loop inductance $\sim 0.5\text{--}2\text{ nH}$, response time $10\text{--}100\text{ ns}$).
4. *Bulk Decoupling*: Polymer tantalum or aluminum electrolytic capacitors ($C_{\text{bulk}} \sim 100\text{--}1000\,\mu\text{F}$, response time $1\text{--}10\,\mu\text{s}$) sustain the rail until the active VRM regulation loop stabilizes.

**Anti-Resonance Voltage Spikes.** Parallel resonance between package inductance $L_{\text{pkg}}$ and board decoupling capacitance creates an anti-resonance impedance peak at frequency $f_{\text{anti}} = 1 / (2\pi \sqrt{L_{\text{pkg}} C_{\text{die}}})$, where PDN impedance spikes to $Z_{\text{anti}} \approx \sqrt{L/C} / \text{ESR}$. If the periodic execution cadence of an attention kernel or vision encoder matches $f_{\text{anti}}$, the resonance amplifies supply voltage oscillations, precipitating gate delay violations or triggering hardware brownout resets.

### Digital logic gate delay and the alpha-power law

In sub-micron CMOS silicon, logic gate propagation delay $t_{\text{prop}}$ is governed by the Sakurai-Newton **alpha-power law**:[^fn-sys-sakurai-droop]
$$ t_{\text{prop}}(V) \propto \frac{C_L \cdot V}{(V - V_{\text{th}})^\alpha} $$
where $C_L$ is the gate load capacitance, $V_{\text{th}}$ is the transistor threshold voltage, and $\alpha \in [1.2, 1.5]$ is the velocity saturation index (contrasting with $\alpha = 2.0$ in long-channel theory).

When rail voltage droops from $V_{\text{nom}}$ to $V_{\text{droop}}$, propagation delay stretches according to:
$$ \frac{t_{\text{prop}}(V_{\text{droop}})}{t_{\text{prop}}(V_{\text{nom}})} = \frac{V_{\text{droop}}}{V_{\text{nom}}} \left( \frac{V_{\text{nom}} - V_{\text{th}}}{V_{\text{droop}} - V_{\text{th}}} \right)^\alpha $$
In a synchronous digital pipeline with clock period $T_{\text{clk}}$, setup time $t_{\text{setup}}$, and clock skew $t_{\text{skew}}$, timing closure requires:
$$ t_{\text{prop}} + t_{\text{setup}} + t_{\text{skew}} \le T_{\text{clk}} $$
Stretching $t_{\text{prop}}$ reduces setup slack. A timing failure occurs only if the measured path crosses its slack limit; a brownout reset depends on a separately configured supervisor threshold. Local decoupling can reduce the rail excursion, subject to its impedance and placement. See @sec-placement-thermal-timing-coupling for the coupled dynamics of power delivery droop, clock frequency throttling, and thermal dissipation on heterogeneous SoCs.

[^fn-sys-sakurai-droop]: **Sakurai-Newton Delay Modeling**\index{Gate delay!Sakurai-Newton model}: The alpha-power law models voltage-dependent gate delay; its parameters are technology dependent. The model predicts reduced setup slack during droop, while a missed deadline, register error, or reset must be established against measured path slack and device thresholds.

## DRAM Contention and Interconnect Arbitration {#sec-appendix-systems-dram}

In cloud machine learning clusters, GPUs utilize high-bandwidth memory (HBM) physically separated from host CPU memory, providing dedicated, uncontended memory channels for deep learning kernels. In embedded robotics SoCs, however, system architectures rely on Unified Memory Architecture (UMA) to satisfy size, weight, and power (SWaP) constraints. Application CPU cores, neural accelerators, GPU cores, and high-rate PCIe or CSI camera DMA engines all share a single physical DRAM interface. In these shared-memory multi-core platforms, DMA transfers and vision prefetching compete directly with the permission path for memory controller command queues and physical DRAM banks.

### DRAM bank organization and conflict latency

A modern DRAM chip (LPDDR5 or DDR5) is organized into multiple independent banks (typically 16 to 32 banks), each possessing a single row buffer composed of sensitive sense amplifiers. Accessing storage cells requires three sequential microarchitectural operations:\index{Memory contention!DRAM bank conflicts}\index{Memory contention!row buffer management}
1. **Row precharge** ($t_{\text{RP}}$): Restores charge to capacitive memory cells and closes the currently open row buffer (typically $14\text{ ns}$).
2. **Row activate** ($t_{\text{RCD}}$): Reads an entire page of storage cells (e.g., 2 KB to 8 KB) into the bank's open row buffer ($14\text{ ns}$).
3. **Column access** ($t_{\text{CAS}} / t_{\text{CL}}$): Reads or writes data beats from the open row buffer onto the memory bus ($14\text{ ns}$).

**The Bank Conflict Penalty.** When consecutive memory operations target different rows within the same physical bank—a *bank conflict*—the memory controller cannot immediately access the column. It must execute a precharge followed by an activate before issuing the column command, introducing a compulsory stall:
$$ \Delta t_{\text{conflict}} \approx t_{\text{RP}} + t_{\text{RCD}} $$
Furthermore, the minimum time between consecutive row activations to the same bank is governed by the row cycle time $t_{\text{RC}} = t_{\text{RAS}} + t_{\text{RP}} \approx 45\text{--}60\text{ ns}$.

When a dense foundation model streaming weights across DRAM rows intersects with high-rate camera DMA writes and a real-time permission thread reading sensor states, repeated row-buffer misses transform low-latency reads into multi-hundred-nanosecond stalls.[^fn-sys-dram-conflicts]

[^fn-sys-dram-conflicts]: **DRAM Bank-Conflict Penalties**\index{Memory contention!DRAM bank conflicts}: A row change in one bank can add precharge and activate time. Video DMA can also queue transactions ahead of a safety read. The resulting delay must be bounded for the specific address mapping, arbitration policy, and workload; a fixed penalty per request is generally unjustified.

### Interconnect crossbars and burst contention

On-chip interconnect fabrics (such as ARM CoreLink AXI4 crossbars or Network-on-Chip (NoC) meshes) split high-bandwidth accelerator and camera DMA transactions into bounded bursts of up to $A_{\text{len}} = 256$ beats. In a shared crossbar without real-time prioritization, transactions enter a FIFO or weighted round-robin queue. For $K$ competing accelerator transactions admitted ahead of a safety-critical permission request, the queuing transfer latency is:
$$ t_{\text{queue,ideal}} = \frac{\sum_{k=1}^K B_k}{\text{BW}_{\text{bus}}} $$
Adding physical bank-switch penalties $\sum \Delta t_{\text{conflict}}$, refresh overhead ($t_{\text{RFC}}$ stalls where all banks are locked for $200\text{--}400\text{ ns}$ every $3.9\,\mu\text{s}$), and bus turnaround penalties, the safety read latency can expand by more than $10\times$ under heavy cognitive load.

To protect real-time control paths against memory contention, embedded systems implement two hardware defenses:
1. *AXI Quality of Service (QoS) Priority Elevation*: The memory interconnect enforces 4-bit `AxQOS` signals, assigning highest priority (`0xF`) to the safety monitor's read channels to enable head-of-line priority preemption over best-effort DMA traffic (`0x0`).
2. *On-Chip SRAM Isolation*: Critical safety states, barrier function parameters, and active trajectory splines bypass external DRAM entirely, executing exclusively out of static on-chip SRAM or Data Tightly Coupled Memory (DTCM).

## Clock Synchronization and Network Timestamps {#sec-appendix-systems-ptp}

In distributed machine learning clusters, nodes synchronize system clocks via Network Time Protocol (NTP) primarily for coarse event logging and telemetry, while parallel training algorithms synchronize execution through communication barriers (such as NCCL AllReduce). In physical AI systems, however, time directly maps to physical space: when a robot moves at $30\text{ m/s}$, a $1\text{ ms}$ synchronization error produces $3\text{ cm}$ of spatial displacement, warping sensor fusion point clouds and invalidating safety clearance buffers. Distributed perception pipelines must convert sensor timestamps into a common clock domain with a measured conversion-error bound.

### Precision time protocol message exchange

The IEEE 1588 Precision Time Protocol (PTP) and IEEE 802.1AS (generalized PTP) synchronize a Slave clock ($S$) to a Master clock ($M$) by exchanging four physical timestamps across the communication link:\index{Precision Time Protocol!clock synchronization}\index{Precision Time Protocol!delay measurement}
1. $t_1$: Master transmits a *Sync* frame, recording its local transmission timestamp.
2. $t_2$: Slave receives the *Sync* frame, recording its local arrival timestamp.
3. $t_3$: Slave transmits a *Delay_Req* frame, recording its local transmission timestamp.
4. $t_4$: Master receives the *Delay_Req* frame, recording its local arrival timestamp.

Under the assumption of clock stability and symmetric forward and reverse propagation delay ($D_{M \to S} = D_{S \to M} = D$), the time relationships satisfy:
$$ t_2 = t_1 + O + D $$
$$ t_4 = t_3 - O + D $$
where $O$ is the slave-minus-master clock offset. The estimated clock offset is:
$$ O = \frac{(t_2 - t_1) - (t_4 - t_3)}{2} $$
The one-way network propagation delay is:
$$ D = \frac{(t_2 - t_1) + (t_4 - t_3)}{2} $$

**Path Asymmetry and Conversion Uncertainty.** If forward and reverse path delays are asymmetric ($\Delta D_{\text{asym}} = D_{M \to S} - D_{S \to M} \ne 0$), the calculated offset incurs an unobservable systematic bias of $\Delta D_{\text{asym}} / 2$. Residual clock uncertainty $\epsilon_{\text{ptp}}$—combining asymmetric propagation, oscillator frequency drift between sync intervals, and hardware timestamp quantization—is explicitly bounded:
$$ \epsilon_{\text{ptp}} \le \frac{|\Delta D_{\text{asym}}|}{2} + \Delta t_{\text{interval}} \cdot \left| \frac{\Delta f}{f_{\text{nom}}} \right| + 2 \tau_{\text{quant}} $$
This conversion bound is stored directly in the proposal header's `sync_error_ns` field (@tbl-appendix-systems-wire-header) and added to every evidence-age calculation in the 1 kHz permission path.

### Physical layer hardware timestamping

Software-based timestamping—where timestamps are captured inside the OS network socket layer or interrupt service routine—suffers from variable kernel queueing, driver interrupt latency, and thread scheduling jitter, injecting $50\,\mu\text{s}$ to $5\text{ ms}$ of non-deterministic timing error.

To eliminate host dispatch error, physical AI hardware utilizes **Physical Layer (PHY) Hardware Timestamping**.[^fn-sys-ptp-timestamps] Dedicated timestamping units in the Ethernet PHY or media access control (MAC) controller capture hardware counter values at the exact instant the physical Start of Frame Delimiter (SFD) crosses the Media Independent Interface (MII / RGMII). This bypasses the entire software stack, reducing timestamping jitter to $< 10\text{ ns}$.

[^fn-sys-ptp-timestamps]: **Hardware Timestamping**\index{Precision Time Protocol!hardware timestamping}: A compatible PHY or MAC timestamps frames closer to the wire than a software interrupt handler. Hardware timestamping removes one source of dispatch variation, while path asymmetry and clock conversion remain. Timestamp uncertainty belongs in the physical belief record and permission budget.

## Heterogeneous SoC Mailboxes and Memory Barriers {#sec-appendix-systems-ipc}

In distributed machine learning systems, inter-process communication occurs across network sockets, gRPC, or direct GPU-to-GPU memory copies over PCIe or NVLink (such as CUDA IPC). On heterogeneous robotics SoCs, however, architectures integrate high-performance application processor cores running Linux (hosting deep neural policy inference) with an isolated real-time safety processor (such as an Arm Cortex-R52 or Cortex-M7) on the same silicon die. Communication across this boundary relies on shared SRAM mailboxes or lock-free ring buffers signaled via hardware doorbells. Because modern application processors feature aggressive out-of-order execution pipelines and weakly ordered memory models (contrasting with x86 Total Store Order), their communication contract must explicitly specify memory ownership, cache maintenance, publication ordering, and hardware memory barriers.

### Remote processor messaging over shared SRAM

An illustrative shared-memory mailbox works as follows:\index{Inter-core communication!RPMSG framework}\index{Memory barrier!ARM weakly ordered model}
1. Core A (Application Processor) writes a message payload to a fixed buffer in shared SRAM.
2. Core A makes the payload visible to Core B using the platform's coherent mapping or explicit cache maintenance and ordering.
3. Core A triggers an inter-processor interrupt (IPI) by writing to Core B's hardware mailbox register.
4. Core B checks publication order, integrity, age, and permission before using the payload.

Linux [RPMsg](https://docs.kernel.org/staging/rpmsg.html) is a virtio-based messaging framework that may use shared memory and a platform-specific kick. It does not prescribe this fixed-buffer protocol or a universal latency bound.

### CPU pipeline reordering and memory fences

In weakly ordered memory architectures (such as ARMv8-A and ARMv9-A), processors do not guarantee that memory writes will be observed by other cores in program order. Out-of-order execution engines and asynchronous write buffers can reorder stores to non-dependent addresses:
```c
// Core A (Application Processor); q_target and q_cmd are joint_target_t structs
shared_buffer->q_target = q_cmd; // Store 1: Payload (struct copy)
mailbox_doorbell = 1;            // Store 2: Interrupt trigger
```
If the CPU reorders Store 2 ahead of Store 1, Core B receives the interrupt before the new joint target is committed to physical memory, reading stale or torn data.

**Hardware Memory Barriers and Shareability Domains.** To enforce deterministic ordering across heterogeneous cores, developers must insert architectural memory barriers:\index{Memory barrier!instruction ordering}
```c
shared_buffer->q_target = q_cmd; // Struct copy of the joint targets
__asm__ volatile("dmb oshst" ::: "memory"); // Outer-shareable store barrier
mailbox_doorbell = 1;            // Assert doorbell register
```
In ARM architectures, barriers operate over explicit shareability domains:
* `DMB ISHST` (Inner Shareable Store): Orders stores across cores within the local application CPU cluster sharing a coherent L2/L3 cache.
* `DMB OSHST` / `DMB OSH` (Outer Shareable): Enforces ordering across the entire system-on-chip, including the real-time Cortex-R/M cores, GPU, and DMA subsystems.
* *Cache Maintenance Operations*: If the shared SRAM is mapped as cached memory, Core A must explicitly clean the cache line to the Point of Coherency (`DC CVAC`) before asserting the doorbell, and Core B must invalidate its local cache line (`DC IVAC`) before reading. Alternatively, mapping the shared mailbox region as Normal Non-Cacheable memory eliminates cache maintenance overhead while retaining barrier-enforced store ordering. See @sec-nervous-mailbox-exchanges and @sec-placement-two-paths-one-die for heterogeneous SoC communication architectures and isolation guarantees.[^fn-sys-memory-barriers]

[^fn-sys-memory-barriers]: **Hardware Memory Barriers**\index{Memory barrier!instruction ordering}: Barriers order accesses only within their specified shareability and memory-attribute contract. On a noncoherent route, cache clean/invalidate operations or coherent mappings are also required. [Arm's memory-ordering guide](https://developer.arm.com/community/arm-community-blogs/b/architectures-and-processors-blog/posts/memory-access-ordering-part-3---memory-access-ordering-in-the-arm-architecture) distinguishes ordering from coherence.

## Actuator Electrical and Thermal Dynamics {#sec-appendix-systems-actuators}

In reinforcement learning and simulation environments (such as MuJoCo or Isaac Gym), policy actions are typically abstracted as instantaneous torque or position commands applied at discrete simulation steps. In physical systems, however, actuators convert electrical energy into mechanical work through electromagnetic Lorentz forces, subject to coupled electrical, thermal, and kinematic constraints.

### Stator electrical rise time

A brushless permanent-magnet synchronous motor (PMSM / BLDC) phase winding exhibits phase resistance $R_{\text{phase}}$ and phase inductance $L_{\text{phase}}$. Applying terminal voltage $V_{\text{terminal}}$ against back-electromotive force $e_{\text{bemf}} = K_e \omega_m$ yields the first-order stator current ODE:\index{Actuator!electrical rise time}\index{Field-Oriented Control!dq-frame dynamics}
$$ L_{\text{phase}} \frac{dI(t)}{dt} + R_{\text{phase}} I(t) = V_{\text{terminal}} - K_e \omega_m $$

In three-phase synchronous machines under Field-Oriented Control (FOC), the stator currents are transformed from the three-phase $abc$ frame into the orthogonal rotor synchronous $dq$ reference frame via the Clarke and Park transformations:
$$ V_d = R_{\text{phase}} I_d + L_d \frac{dI_d}{dt} - \omega_e L_q I_q $$
$$ V_q = R_{\text{phase}} I_q + L_q \frac{dI_q}{dt} + \omega_e L_d I_d + \omega_e \lambda_{\text{pm}} $$
where $\omega_e = p \omega_m$ is electrical angular velocity ($p$ pole pairs), $\lambda_{\text{pm}}$ is the rotor permanent-magnet flux linkage, and $L_d, L_q$ are direct and quadrature axis inductances. Under standard constant torque-angle control ($I_d = 0$), electromagnetic torque is directly proportional to quadrature current:
$$ \tau_{\text{motor}} = \frac{3}{2} p \, \lambda_{\text{pm}} I_q = K_t I_q $$

For a commanded voltage step applied from rest ($\omega_m = 0$), quadrature current rises exponentially:
$$ I_q(t) = \frac{V_{\text{terminal}}}{R_{\text{phase}}} \left( 1 - e^{-t / \tau_e} \right), \quad \tau_e = \frac{L_q}{R_{\text{phase}}} $$
where $\tau_e$ is the electrical time constant. Current—and therefore delivered torque—reaches approximately 63 percent of its steady-state value after one time constant $\tau_e$ (typically $200\,\mu\text{s}$ to $2\text{ ms}$ in robotics actuators). An unprivileged neural policy step command cannot produce an instantaneous step in physical torque.

### Lumped thermal networks and duty cycle

Current flowing through stator windings dissipates resistive Joule heat:
$$ P_{\text{loss}}(t) = \frac{3}{2} I_q^2(t) R_{\text{phase}}(T) $$
where copper electrical resistance increases linearly with temperature:
$$ R_{\text{phase}}(T) = R_0 \left[ 1 + \alpha_{\text{Cu}} (T - T_0) \right] $$
with temperature coefficient $\alpha_{\text{Cu}} \approx 0.00393\text{ K}^{-1}$ for copper.

**Multi-Node Lumped Thermal Networks.** In a physical motor, thermal dynamics span multiple physical interfaces with disparate thermal masses:\index{Actuator!stator thermal dynamics}\index{Actuator!thermal ladder network}

1. *Stator Winding Copper*: Low thermal capacitance $C_{\text{cu}}$, rapid heating from Joule dissipation ($\tau_{\text{cu}} \sim 10\text{--}30\text{ s}$).
2. *Stator Iron Laminations*: Moderate thermal capacitance $C_{\text{iron}}$, absorbing iron eddy-current and hysteresis losses $P_{\text{iron}} \propto \omega_e^{1.5} B^2$ and heat conducted across winding insulation $R_{\text{th,cu-iron}}$.
3. *Motor Frame and Aluminum Housing*: Large thermal capacitance $C_{\text{case}}$, conducting heat into the robotic link structure and convecting to ambient air through $R_{\text{th,case-amb}}$ ($\tau_{\text{case}} \sim 10\text{--}30\text{ min}$).

The temperature dynamics across these nodes satisfy the coupled differential system:
$$ C_{\text{cu}} \frac{dT_{\text{cu}}}{dt} = P_{\text{loss}}(t) - \frac{T_{\text{cu}} - T_{\text{iron}}}{R_{\text{th,cu-iron}}} $$
$$ C_{\text{iron}} \frac{dT_{\text{iron}}}{dt} = \frac{T_{\text{cu}} - T_{\text{iron}}}{R_{\text{th,cu-iron}}} + P_{\text{iron}} - \frac{T_{\text{iron}} - T_{\text{case}}}{R_{\text{th,iron-case}}} $$
$$ C_{\text{case}} \frac{dT_{\text{case}}}{dt} = \frac{T_{\text{iron}} - T_{\text{case}}}{R_{\text{th,iron-case}}} - \frac{T_{\text{case}} - T_{\text{ambient}}}{R_{\text{th,case-amb}}} $$

In a simplified single-node lumped thermal model with effective thermal resistance to ambient $\theta_{JA}$ (in $\text{K/W}$) and thermal heat capacity $C_{\text{th}}$ (in $\text{J/K}$), temperature rise $\Delta T(t) = T_{\text{winding}}(t) - T_{\text{ambient}}$ satisfies:[^fn-sys-motor-heating]
$$ C_{\text{th}} \frac{d\Delta T(t)}{dt} = P_{\text{loss}}(t) - \frac{\Delta T(t)}{\theta_{JA}} $$
Under constant power, temperature rises with thermal time constant $\tau_{\text{th}} = \theta_{JA} C_{\text{th}}$:
$$ \Delta T(t) = P_{\text{loss}} \theta_{JA} \left( 1 - e^{-t / \tau_{\text{th}}} \right) $$
