**Continuous Torque vs. Transient Overdrive.** Continuous torque capacity $\tau_{\text{cont}}$ is bounded by the maximum allowable winding temperature rise $\Delta T_{\max}$:
$$ \tau_{\text{cont}} \le K_t \sqrt{\frac{\Delta T_{\max}}{\theta_{JA} R_{\text{phase}}}} $$
Transient torque peaks $\tau_{\text{peak}} \approx 2\text{--}4 \times \tau_{\text{cont}}$ are permitted during aggressive dynamic maneuvers only if an active digital $I^2 t$ thermal protection observer running on the safety microcontroller bounds the thermal integral:
$$ \Delta T[k+1] = \Delta T[k] e^{-\Delta t / \tau_{\text{th}}} + \theta_{JA} P_{\text{loss}}[k] \left( 1 - e^{-\Delta t / \tau_{\text{th}}} \right) $$
When estimated winding temperature approaches the dielectric breakdown limit ($180^\circ\text{C}$ Class H insulation) or rotor neodymium magnet demagnetization threshold ($80\text{--}120^\circ\text{C}$), the permission filter clamps commanded current, preventing catastrophic actuator destruction.

[^fn-sys-motor-heating]: **Stator Thermal Time Constants**\index{Actuator!stator thermal dynamics}: Resistive Joule heating elevates motor phase winding temperatures during continuous high-torque maneuvers. Because copper electrical resistivity increases linearly with temperature, hot windings exhibit higher resistance, reducing torque output under terminal voltage saturation. Exceeding winding insulation temperature limits breaks down dielectric coatings, causing inter-turn short circuits and irreversible actuator destruction.

### Reflected rotor inertia and angular jerk limits {#sec-appendix-systems-rotor-jerk}

Geared electromagnetic actuators amplify delivered motor torque while multiplying rotor inertia at the joint output. For a transmission with gear reduction ratio $N = \omega_{\text{motor}} / \omega_{\text{joint}}$, kinetic energy conservation dictates the reflected inertia acting at the output link:\index{Reflected rotor inertia!kinetic energy derivation}\index{Angular jerk!electromechanical limits}
$$ E_k = \frac{1}{2} J_{\text{rotor}} \omega_{\text{motor}}^2 + \frac{1}{2} J_{\text{load}} \omega_{\text{joint}}^2 = \frac{1}{2} (J_{\text{load}} + N^2 J_{\text{rotor}}) \dot{q}^2 $$
The effective rotational inertia seen at joint coordinate $q$ is:
$$ J_{\text{eff}} = J_{\text{load}} + N^2 J_{\text{rotor}} $$
The joint equation of motion under motor electromagnetic torque $\tau_{\text{motor}}$ is:
$$ \ddot{q} = \frac{N \tau_{\text{motor}} - \tau_{\text{ext}}}{J_{\text{load}} + N^2 J_{\text{rotor}}} $$
Differentiating $\ddot{q}$ with respect to gear ratio $N$ at zero external load yields:
$$ \frac{\partial \ddot{q}}{\partial N} = \frac{\tau_{\text{motor}} (J_{\text{load}} - N^2 J_{\text{rotor}})}{(J_{\text{load}} + N^2 J_{\text{rotor}})^2} $$
Setting $\frac{\partial \ddot{q}}{\partial N} = 0$ yields the **inertia-matching ratio** $N^* = \sqrt{J_{\text{load}} / J_{\text{rotor}}}$. When $N > N^*$, counter-intuitively, increasing the gear ratio decreases delivered joint acceleration because the motor spends the majority of its torque accelerating its own rotor rather than the link.

#### Dynamic angular jerk and torque slew limits

Angular jerk $j_{\text{joint}}(t) = \dddot{q}(t)$ measures the time rate of change of joint acceleration:
$$ j_{\text{joint}}(t) = \frac{N}{J_{\text{load}} + N^2 J_{\text{rotor}}} \frac{d\tau_{\text{motor}}(t)}{dt} $$
Electromagnetic torque relates to stator quadrature current via torque constant $K_t$: $\tau_{\text{motor}} = K_t I_q$. From the stator electrical dynamics in this section, current slew rate is bounded by winding inductance $L_{\text{phase}}$:
$$ \frac{d\tau_{\text{motor}}}{dt} = K_t \frac{dI_q}{dt} = \frac{K_t}{L_{\text{phase}}} \left( V_{\text{terminal}} - K_e \omega_m - R_{\text{phase}} I_q \right) $$
Under maximum DC bus terminal voltage saturation $V_{\max}$, the physical upper bound on delivered angular jerk is:
$$ |j_{\max}| \le \frac{N K_t (V_{\max} - K_e \omega_m)}{L_{\text{phase}} (J_{\text{load}} + N^2 J_{\text{rotor}})} $$
When an unprivileged neural policy outputs a step torque discontinuity $\Delta \boldsymbol{\tau}$ across discrete timesteps, the commanded derivative $\frac{d\tau}{dt} \to \infty$ cannot be delivered instantaneously by physical silicon. The inverter enters hard voltage saturation, causing steep current slew ($dI/dt$), intense thermal stress on power MOSFETs, and shock loads across gear-tooth contact flanks ($\sigma_b \propto W_t / (b m Y)$). Synchronous pre-actuation invariant filters evaluate numerical torque derivatives $(\boldsymbol{\tau}[k] - \boldsymbol{\tau}[k-1]) / \Delta t$ to ensure requested actions remain within allowable jerk envelopes before latching power stages.

## DC Bus Power Distribution and Energy Absorption {#sec-appendix-systems-power}

In data center machine learning clusters, electrical power is managed by high-capacity facility uninterruptible power supplies (UPS) and dedicated substation transformers. On mobile autonomous platforms, computational accelerators and mechanical actuators draw from a shared, finite DC power distribution network. A robotic platform's electrical power distribution network must supply acceleration surges and absorb regenerative braking energy across finite bus capacitance and harness impedance.

### Inductive droop and capacitive decoupling

When multiple high-torque actuators accelerate simultaneously, the total load current steps by $\Delta I_{\text{load}} = \sum \Delta I_k$ with steep current slew rates $dI_{\text{load}}/dt$. The electrical wiring harness connecting the main battery to distributed joint inverters possesses parasitic loop inductance $L_{\text{bus}}$ and harness resistance $R_{\text{bus}}$. These parasitics impede source current delivery, producing instantaneous inductive rail droop at the actuator inverter terminals:\index{Inductive voltage droop!DC bus harness}\index{Decoupling capacitors!inverter DC bus}
$$ \Delta V_{\text{bus}}(t) = R_{\text{bus}} I_{\text{source}}(t) + L_{\text{bus}} \frac{dI_{\text{source}}}{dt} + \Delta V_C(t) $$
Local inverter bus capacitance $C_{\text{bus}}$ must supply the instantaneous deficit between load demand and source current:
$$ \Delta V_C(t) = \frac{1}{C_{\text{bus}}} \int_0^t \left( I_{\text{load}}(s) - I_{\text{source}}(s) \right) ds $$

If the DC bus terminal voltage drops below the drive's configured Under-Voltage Lockout (UVLO) threshold $V_{\text{UVLO}}$, the gate driver power silicon disables itself to prevent erratic MOSFET gate switching, dropping motor torque instantly. To maintain bus voltage stability during a step acceleration of duration $\Delta t_{\text{step}}$, the minimum local decoupling capacitance is bounded by:
$$ C_{\text{bus}} \ge \frac{\Delta I_{\text{step}} \cdot \Delta t_{\text{step}}}{2 \Delta V_{\text{droop, max}}} $$
Local capacitor banks combine low-ESR multi-layer ceramic capacitors (MLCCs) for high-frequency ripple filtering ($20\text{--}100\text{ kHz}$ inverter switching) with bulk electrolytic or polymer capacitors for transient step energy buffering.

### Regenerative braking surges and chopper sizing

During controlled regenerative deceleration or emergency stopping, mechanical kinetic energy $E_k = \frac{1}{2} m v^2$ (linear platform motion) or $E_k = \frac{1}{2} J_{\text{eff}} \dot{q}^2$ (articulated joint rotation) is converted back into electrical energy by the motor acting as a generator. Current flows back through the inverter bridge into the DC bus via active synchronous rectification or freewheeling body diodes.\index{Regenerative braking!chopper resistor}\index{Power electronics!brake chopper}

If the battery cannot accept this regenerative current—such as when the battery pack is at 100 percent state-of-charge ($> 4.2\text{ V/cell}$), when battery internal resistance rises at freezing temperatures, or when safety contactors open to isolate the pack—the returned electrical energy $\eta_{\text{regen}} E_k$ is forced into the local bus capacitor $C_{\text{bus}}$. The resulting terminal voltage surge follows the ideal capacitor relationship:
$$ \Delta E_C = \frac{1}{2} C_{\text{bus}} \left( V_{\text{final}}^2 - V_{\text{initial}}^2 \right) = \eta_{\text{regen}} E_k $$
$$ V_{\text{final}} = \sqrt{ V_{\text{initial}}^2 + \frac{2 \eta_{\text{regen}} E_k}{C_{\text{bus}}} } $$

If $V_{\text{final}}$ exceeds the MOSFET drain-source breakdown voltage $V_{\text{DSS}}$ or the inverter Over-Voltage Lockout (OVLO) threshold, the power semiconductors enter destructive avalanche breakdown.

**Dynamic Brake Choppers.** To prevent overvoltage destruction, motor drives incorporate an active **dynamic brake chopper**. When DC bus voltage crosses a hardware clamp threshold $V_{\text{clamp}}$, a high-power semiconductor switch (MOSFET or IGBT) modulates an auxiliary low-inductance braking resistor $R_{\text{brake}}$ to burn excess kinetic energy as heat:[^fn-sys-brake-chopper]
$$ R_{\text{brake}} \le \frac{V_{\text{clamp}}^2}{P_{\text{regen, peak}}} $$
$$ P_{\text{regen, peak}} \approx \eta_{\text{regen}} \cdot \tau_{\text{brake}} \cdot \omega_{\max} $$
In addition to peak power sizing, the braking resistor must be rated for single-pulse adiabatic energy absorption:
$$ E_{\text{pulse}} \ge \eta_{\text{regen}} E_k $$
with a thermal cooldown time constant that prevents cumulative thermal failure during repeated stop-and-go duty cycles.

[^fn-sys-brake-chopper]: **Dynamic Braking Choppers**\index{Regenerative braking!chopper resistor}: A qualified chopper can dissipate returned energy when the battery is unavailable as a sink. Its threshold, switch and resistor ratings, pulse duration, and thermal recovery must be tested. Regeneration and chopper operation are not inherent to every emergency stop; safe torque off can instead leave a motor coasting.

## Real-Time Fieldbuses and Lock-Free Synchronization {#sec-appendix-systems-fieldbus}

In distributed machine learning clusters, networks are built on high-bandwidth fabrics (such as 100/400 Gbps RoCEv2 or InfiniBand) optimized for aggregate data-parallel throughput via credit-based flow control. In physical AI systems, however, the onboard communication fabric must simultaneously multiplex two diametrically opposed traffic classes:
1. *High-bandwidth best-effort perception streams*: Multi-gigabit video from high-resolution GMSL2/GigE Vision cameras ($2\text{--}8\text{ Gbps}$) and 3D lidar point clouds ($100\text{--}1000\text{ Mbps}$) streaming into the AI accelerator's unified memory for foundation model inference.
2. *Hard real-time periodic control traffic*: Deterministic 1 kHz joint setpoint commands and high-resolution torque/position feedback ($100\text{--}500\text{ kbps}$) exchanged with distributed motor inverters.

If these two traffic classes share a naive best-effort Ethernet fabric with first-in, first-out (FIFO) queueing, multi-megabyte perception bursts cause severe queue congestion and buffer bloat. A burst of video frames can delay a motor control packet by $5\text{--}20\text{ ms}$—violating the 1 ms control deadline, starving the inverter current loop, and tripping hardware emergency stops. Coordinating distributed drives while ingesting perception streams requires an architectural separation of fabrics, deterministic bus schedules, and bounded lock-free publication protocols.

### Fieldbus serialization and schedulability

On shared physical buses, $N_{\text{axes}}$ actuator drives transmit telemetry and receive setpoints cyclically. To prevent perception traffic from corrupting motor timing, physical AI architectures utilize dedicated deterministic fieldbuses (CAN FD or EtherCAT) or time-scheduled switched Ethernet (IEEE TSN).\index{Fieldbus!CAN-FD arbitration}\index{Fieldbus!CAN-FD WCRT}\index{Fieldbus!EtherCAT on-the-fly}

**CAN FD Dual-Rate Bit Timing and Arbitration.** Controller Area Network with Flexible Data-Rate (CAN FD, ISO 11898-1) extends classical CAN by introducing dual bit-rate switching and expanding payload capacity from 8 bytes up to 64 bytes:

* *Arbitration Phase*: Transmitted at the nominal bit rate $R_{\text{nom}}$ (typically $500\text{ kbps}$ or $1\text{ Mbps}$). The bit time $T_{\text{bit,nom}} = 1/R_{\text{nom}}$ must accommodate physical cable propagation delays across the robot chassis and transceiver delays ($2 t_{\text{prop}} + t_{\text{transceiver}}$), allowing non-destructive bitwise priority arbitration. Nodes drive the bus using dominant (logic 0) or recessive (logic 1) states. If two nodes transmit simultaneously, the lower numerical message identifier (higher logical priority) overwrites recessive bits, winning the bus without collision or frame destruction.
* *Data Phase*: Once arbitration is established, the winning node asserts the Bit Rate Switch (BRS) bit, accelerating transmission to the data bit rate $R_{\text{data}}$ (typically $2\text{--}8\text{ Mbps}$). Because only a single node drives the bus during the data phase, physical propagation delay between distributed nodes no longer constrains bit duration.
* *Bit-Stuffing Overhead*: To preserve transceiver clock synchronization, the physical layer inserts a dynamic stuff bit after every 5 consecutive identical bits in the arbitration phase, alongside fixed stuff bits embedded within the CRC field.

The serialization duration for frame $i$ is:
$$ t_{\text{frame},i} \approx \frac{B_{\text{arb},i}}{R_{\text{nom}}} + \frac{B_{\text{data},i}}{R_{\text{data}}} + t_{\text{stuff},i} + t_{\text{interframe},i} $$
where $B_{\text{arb},i}$ is the arbitration field length (identifier, control bits), $B_{\text{data},i}$ is the payload and CRC length, $t_{\text{stuff},i}$ accounts for stuff bits, and $t_{\text{interframe},i}$ is the minimum 3-bit inter-frame spacing.

**CAN FD Worst-Case Response Time (WCRT).** Because CAN FD frames are non-preemptive—a transmission in progress cannot be aborted when a higher-priority message is released—the worst-case response time $R_i$ of periodic control frame $i$ is evaluated via Tindell's recurrence:
$$ R_i = C_i + B_i + \sum_{j \in hp(i)} \left\lceil \frac{R_i + J_j + \tau_{\text{bit}}}{T_j} \right\rceil C_j $$
where $C_i = t_{\text{frame},i}$, $J_j$ is the release jitter of higher-priority message $j$, and $B_i$ is the maximum lower-priority blocking duration:
$$ B_i = \max_{k \in lp(i)} C_k $$
Because a maximum 64-byte CAN FD frame at $2\text{ Mbps}$ requires approximately $300\text{--}400\,\mu\text{s}$ to serialize, a CAN FD bus at $80\%$ utilization can service at most $10\text{--}15$ joint axes at 1 kHz. CAN FD cannot carry raw camera or lidar perception data; its role is strictly bounded to joint-level motor and sensor communication.

**EtherCAT On-the-Fly Ring Processing.** For high-axis-count systems (such as humanoids with 30 to 50 degrees of freedom), EtherCAT (ETG.1000) achieves deterministic 1 kHz to 10 kHz cycle times over standard 100BASE-TX full-duplex Ethernet ($R_{\text{link}} = 100\text{ Mbps}$). Rather than transmitting individual frames per axis, EtherCAT structures communication as an active logical ring:

1. The real-time master (executing on the safety microcontroller or `PREEMPT_RT` Linux host) transmits a single standard Ethernet frame (EtherType `0x88A4`) traversing all slave drives in a physical daisy chain.
2. Each drive integrates an EtherCAT Slave Controller (ESC) application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC) (such as Beckhoff ET1100 or field-programmable gate array (FPGA) IP). As the frame's bits pass through the ESC's physical shift registers, the ESC **processes data on the fly**:
   - It reads commanded setpoints (joint target position, velocity, and feedforward torque) directly from its allocated byte offset in the datagram.
   - It writes actual measured feedback (encoder position, phase current, and drive status flags) into the moving frame.
3. The internal hardware processing latency per slave is strictly bounded ($t_{\text{slave},s} \approx 1.0\,\mu\text{s}$), and the frame is automatically looped back by the final slave on the second Ethernet pair.

The total round-trip cycle period for $S$ slave drives is bounded by:
$$ T_{\text{cycle}} \ge \frac{B_{\text{frame}}}{R_{\text{link}}} + t_{\text{master}} + \sum_{s=1}^S t_{\text{slave},s} + t_{\text{prop}} + t_{\text{guard}} $$
For a 30-axis humanoid exchanging 8 bytes of command setpoints and 12 bytes of feedback per joint, the entire cyclic exchange ($600\text{ bytes}$) fits comfortably within a single $750\text{-byte}$ Ethernet frame. The complete round-trip across all 30 axes executes in approximately $65\,\mu\text{s}$ at $100\text{ Mbps}$, consuming less than $7\%$ of the 1 ms control period. Furthermore, EtherCAT **Distributed Clocks (DC)** synchronize all slave timers to the master with sub-microsecond precision ($< 100\text{ ns}$ clock skew) by measuring and compensating for physical cable propagation delays, enabling synchronous PWM carrier generation across all inverter drives.

### Time-sensitive networking and scheduled ethernet gates

While EtherCAT processes frames on the fly through specialized slave controllers, modern multi-camera and lidar robotic systems require multi-gigabit Ethernet fabrics that transport high-bandwidth vision data alongside hard real-time actuator commands. IEEE **Time-Sensitive Networking (TSN)** provides deterministic Ethernet via standards that bound queuing jitter and reserve transmission windows:\index{Fieldbus!Time-Sensitive Networking}\index{Time-Sensitive Networking!Time-Aware Shaper}\index{Time-Sensitive Networking!frame preemption}

**IEEE 802.1Qbv Time-Aware Shaper (TAS).** TAS coordinates traffic transmission using hardware-controlled transmission gates associated with each priority egress queue (traffic classes 0 to 7). A cyclic **Gate Control List (GCL)**—synchronized across all network bridges via IEEE 802.1AS (generalized Precision Time Protocol)—switches gates open or closed at precise physical time epochs. By reserving dedicated time windows exclusively for high-priority Scheduled Traffic (ST), TAS eliminates queuing interference from lower-priority Best-Effort (BE) traffic.

**Guard Bands and Frame Preemption.** Standard Ethernet frames are non-preemptive: once a transmission begins, it cannot be interrupted on physical copper or optical links. If a lower-priority best-effort packet begins transmission immediately before an ST time slice opens, the scheduled frame experiences transmission blocking of up to the maximum frame duration. To prevent this, TAS enforces a **guard band** prior to each scheduled traffic window:
$$ t_{\text{guard}} = \frac{\text{MTU}_{\text{BE}}}{R_{\text{link}}} $$
where $\text{MTU}_{\text{BE}}$ is the maximum transmission unit of best-effort traffic (typically 1,518 bytes, or 9,000 bytes for jumbo frames) and $R_{\text{link}}$ is the physical link bit rate. For a standard 1,518-byte frame on a 1 Gbps link, the guard band lasts:
$$ t_{\text{guard}} = \frac{1518 \times 8\text{ bits}}{10^9\text{ bps}} \approx 12.14\,\mu\text{s} $$
During this guard band, no best-effort frame may begin transmission if it cannot finish before the scheduled gate opens. This creates idle transmission overhead on the physical bus.

To reclaim this unused bandwidth, **IEEE 802.1Qbu and IEEE 802.3br Frame Preemption** divide preemptible (best-effort) MAC frames into fragments of at least 64 bytes. When an express (scheduled) frame arrives, the physical layer interrupts the ongoing preemptible frame, transmits the express frame with minimal latency, and resumes the preempted frame with an mPacket continuation header. Frame preemption reduces the maximum guard band from an entire MTU down to the minimum fragment size:
$$ t_{\text{guard,preempt}} = \frac{123\text{ bytes} \times 8\text{ bits}}{R_{\text{link}}} \approx 0.98\,\mu\text{s} $$
at 1 Gbps, reclaiming more than 90 percent of the lost guard band bandwidth and ensuring that multi-gigabit camera streaming does not inject millisecond-scale jitter into joint actuator control loops.

**Fieldbus Cycle Budget Synthesis.** The achievable control cycle period $T_{\text{cycle}}$ across these three primary fieldbus architectures reflects their distinct arbitration mechanisms:

* **CAN FD**: Cycle time is constrained by serial bitwise arbitration and lower-priority blocking:
$$ T_{\text{cycle}} \ge \sum_{i=1}^{N_{\text{axes}}} t_{\text{frame},i} + \max_{k \in lp} t_{\text{frame},k} + t_{\text{margin}} $$
* **EtherCAT**: Cycle time is constrained by on-the-fly ring forwarding across $S$ slave controllers:
$$ T_{\text{cycle}} \ge \sum_f \frac{B_f}{R_{\text{link}}} + t_{\text{master}} + \sum_{s=1}^S t_{\text{slave},s} + t_{\text{prop}} + t_{\text{guard}} $$
* **TSN (802.1Qbv)**: Cycle time partitions transmission into scheduled and best-effort windows bounded by network synchronization uncertainty:
$$ T_{\text{cycle}} \ge T_{\text{ST}} + t_{\text{guard}} + T_{\text{BE}} + \Delta_{\text{sync}} $$
where $\Delta_{\text{sync}}$ is the maximum clock synchronization skew across network bridges. See @sec-nervous-deterministic-fieldbuses, @sec-nervous-cadences, and @sec-nervous-fieldbus-architectures for hardware fieldbus selection across the nervous system.

### Lock-free seqlocks for multi-rate shared memory

When a producer updates multiword state read by a deadline-bound enforcer, waiting on a producer-held mutex can violate the reader's deadline. The single-slot mailbox in @algo-lock-free-trajectory uses a sequence counter to detect a torn snapshot.

A **sequence counter** marks a single writer's publication in progress with an odd value and a completed publication with an even value:\index{Concurrency!sequence locks}

1. **Writer Protocol**:
   - Publish an odd sequence value, write the payload, and make it visible through the platform's coherent or cache-maintained memory contract.
   - Publish the next even value with release ordering.
2. **Reader Protocol**:
   - Read $S_1$ with acquire ordering. If it is odd, reject this publication without waiting.
   - Make one bounded copy to scratch memory using the platform's required load ordering, then read $S_2$.
   - Accept only if $S_1=S_2$ and both are even, and the copied frame passes integrity, timestamp, and lease checks. Otherwise retain the last validated local command only while its lease and stopping margin permit; then enter the state-matched fallback.

The reader's one-attempt execution time can be bounded on the target hardware; success probability depends on the writer's schedule and cannot be inferred from payload size alone. Conventional Linux seqlock readers may retry, as the [kernel documentation](https://docs.kernel.org/locking/seqlock.html) shows, but a real-time permission gate cannot use an unbounded retry loop.

```pseudocode
#| label: algo-lock-free-trajectory
#| pdf-line-number: true
#| pdf-right-comment: false
#| html-comment-delimiter: "▷"

\begin{algorithm}
\caption{Single-Slot Trajectory Seqlock Baseline}
\begin{algorithmic}
\Require proposal $P$ (proposal header with $\text{sequence\_id}$, $\text{t\_evidence\_ns}$, $\text{sync\_error\_ns}$, $\text{t\_expire\_ns}$; waypoints $\mathbf{w}_{1..K}$; $\text{crc32}$), scratch buffer $B_{\text{scratch}}$ and previously validated active spline $B_{\text{active}}$ in static SRAM, shared SRAM mailbox $(c_{\text{seq}}, \text{Slot}_{\text{shared}})$, current time $t_{\text{now}}$ and evidence-age budget $t_{\text{age,max}}$ (the largest admissible $t_{\text{age}}$), both on the safety microcontroller's clock
\Ensure promoted validated chunk in $B_{\text{active}}$ or rejection with $B_{\text{active}}$ unchanged
\Statex
\Function{PublishActionChunk}{$P$}
    \State $c_{\text{curr}} \gets \Call{AtomicLoadExplicit}{c_{\text{seq}}, \text{memory\_order\_relaxed}}$
    \State $\Call{AtomicStoreExplicit}{c_{\text{seq}}, c_{\text{curr}} + 1, \text{memory\_order\_relaxed}}$ \Comment{mark odd: write in progress}
    \State $\Call{HardwareMemoryBarrier}{\text{DMB\_OSHST}}$ \Comment{outer-shareable store barrier pushes counter}
    \State $\Call{CopyMemory}{\text{Slot}_{\text{shared}}.\text{payload}, P, \text{sizeof}(P)}$ \Comment{copy multi-word trajectory}
    \State $\Call{HardwareMemoryBarrier}{\text{DMB\_OSH}}$ \Comment{outer-shareable full barrier: payload visible}
    \State $\Call{AtomicStoreExplicit}{c_{\text{seq}}, c_{\text{curr}} + 2, \text{memory\_order\_release}}$ \Comment{mark even: publish committed}
\EndFunction
\Statex
\Function{LatchLatestActionChunk}{$B_{\text{scratch}}, B_{\text{active}}, t_{\text{now}}$}
    \State $c_{\text{start}} \gets \Call{AtomicLoadExplicit}{c_{\text{seq}}, \text{memory\_order\_acquire}}$ \Comment{load initial counter (ARM LDAR acquire)}
    \If{$c_{\text{start}}$ is odd}
        \State \Return $\text{STATUS\_WRITER\_ACTIVE}$ \Comment{writer active; retain prior spline}
    \EndIf
    \State $\Call{HardwareMemoryBarrier}{\text{DMB\_OSHLD}}$ \Comment{explicit barrier: prevent payload reads hoisting before counter}
    \State $\Call{CopyMemory}{B_{\text{scratch}}, \text{Slot}_{\text{shared}}.\text{payload}, \text{sizeof}(\text{Payload})}$ \Comment{tentative copy; active spline unchanged}
    \State $\Call{HardwareMemoryBarrier}{\text{DMB\_OSHLD}}$ \Comment{LDAR cannot prevent prior reads sinking; DMB forces payload reads before $c_{\text{end}}$}
    \State $c_{\text{end}} \gets \Call{AtomicLoadExplicit}{c_{\text{seq}}, \text{memory\_order\_acquire}}$ \Comment{re-read sequence counter}
    \If{$c_{\text{start}} \ne c_{\text{end}}$}
        \State \Return $\text{STATUS\_TORN\_READ}$ \Comment{concurrent write detected}
    \EndIf
    \If{$\Call{ComputeCrc32}{B_{\text{scratch}}} \ne B_{\text{scratch}}.\text{crc32}$}
        \State \Return $\text{STATUS\_CHECKSUM\_INVALID}$
    \EndIf
    \If{$t_{\text{now}} \ge B_{\text{scratch}}.\text{t\_expire\_ns}$}
        \State \Return $\text{STATUS\_LEASE\_EXPIRED}$ \Comment{expiry is absolute; the reader may only shorten it}
    \EndIf
    \If{$t_{\text{now}} - B_{\text{scratch}}.\text{t\_evidence\_ns} + B_{\text{scratch}}.\text{sync\_error\_ns} > t_{\text{age,max}}$}
        \State \Return $\text{STATUS\_EVIDENCE\_STALE}$ \Comment{conversion error is added to every age}
    \EndIf
    \State $B_{\text{active}} \gets B_{\text{scratch}}$ \Comment{promote only after sequence, CRC, expiry, and evidence-age checks}
    \State \Return $\text{STATUS\_VALID\_LATCHED}$
\EndFunction
\end{algorithmic}
\end{algorithm}
```

@Sec-nervous-cadences exchanges the proposal header and its chunk payload through this mailbox; @sec-appendix-systems-wire-header gives their byte layout.

## Camera Projective Geometry and Covariance Propagation {#sec-appendix-systems-vision}

In computer vision for machine learning, neural models typically process normalized pixel tensors to predict 2D bounding boxes or semantic segmentation masks. In physical AI systems, however, visual observations must be grounded as physical objects in continuous Euclidean 3D metric space to evaluate spatial clearance buffers $D_{\text{clear}}$ and enforce collision-avoidance invariants. Perception pipelines map continuous Euclidean 3D scenes onto discrete 2D camera photosite grids, and unproject pixel detections back into metric space under quantified measurement uncertainty.

### Intrinsic projection matrix and radial distortion

Under the standard pinhole camera model, a 3D point $\mathbf{p}_c = [x_c, y_c, z_c]^\top$ in camera coordinates projects onto pixel coordinates $\mathbf{u} = [u, v]^\top$ via the intrinsic calibration matrix $\mathbf{K}$:[^fn-sys-pinhole-projection]
$$
\tilde{\mathbf{u}} = \begin{bmatrix} u \\ v \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \frac{1}{z_c} \mathbf{K} \mathbf{p}_c = \frac{1}{z_c} \begin{bmatrix} f_x & 0 & c_x \\ 0 & f_y & c_y \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x_c \\ y_c \\ z_c \end{bmatrix}
$$
where $(f_x, f_y)$ are focal lengths in pixel units and $(c_x, c_y)$ is the principal point. Non-linear radial lens distortion is modeled by distortion coefficients $(k_1, k_2)$:
$$ r^2 = x_n^2 + y_n^2, \quad x_d = x_n (1 + k_1 r^2 + k_2 r^4), \quad y_d = y_n (1 + k_1 r^2 + k_2 r^4) $$
where $(x_n, y_n) = (x_c / z_c, y_c / z_c)$ are normalized image coordinates.

[^fn-sys-pinhole-projection]: **Pinhole Intrinsic Projection**\index{Camera model!pinhole projection}: The pinhole model projects 3D points onto a 2D sensor through calibrated intrinsics. Under fixed pixel noise, the lateral variance after depth unprojection grows with squared distance; depth-error and calibration terms follow their own models. Uncalibrated intrinsics can bias a clearance estimate and must be included in its error envelope.

### Metric unprojection and spatial covariance propagation

When unprojecting a 2D pixel observation $\mathbf{u}$ with measured depth $z$ into 3D camera coordinates, photosite measurement noise $\mathbf{\Sigma}_{\text{meas}} = \text{diag}(\sigma_u^2, \sigma_v^2, \sigma_z^2)$ propagates through the unprojection Jacobian $\mathbf{J}_{\text{unproj}}$:\index{Mathematics!covariance propagation}
$$
\mathbf{p}_c = \begin{bmatrix} (u - c_x) z / f_x \\ (v - c_y) z / f_y \\ z \end{bmatrix}, \quad \mathbf{\Sigma}_c = \mathbf{J}_{\text{unproj}} \mathbf{\Sigma}_{\text{meas}} \mathbf{J}_{\text{unproj}}^\top
$$
Transforming this 3D point into the robot body frame via rigid extrinsic transform $\mathbf{T}_{bc} = [\mathbf{R}_{bc}, \mathbf{p}_{bc}; \mathbf{0}^\top, 1]$ yields the spatial body covariance:
$$ \mathbf{\Sigma}_b = \mathbf{R}_{bc} \mathbf{\Sigma}_c \mathbf{R}_{bc}^\top + \mathbf{\Sigma}_{\text{ext}} $$
where $\mathbf{\Sigma}_{\text{ext}}$ models independent extrinsic uncertainty under this first-order approximation; correlations require the corresponding cross terms. A probabilistic clearance buffer may scale with $\sqrt{\lambda_{\max}(\mathbf{\Sigma}_b)}$ at a declared tail risk. A deterministic permission check instead needs a justified bounded-error envelope; covariance alone does not give a worst-case bound.

### Zhang's planar homography and camera calibration

Zhang's calibration technique computes the camera intrinsic matrix $\mathbf{K}$ by observing a planar calibration rig (such as a checkerboard pattern) across $N \ge 3$ distinct orientations [@zhang2000flexible]. Without loss of generality, assume the model plane lies on $Z = 0$ in world coordinates. A 3D model point $\mathbf{M} = [X, Y, 0, 1]^\top$ maps to a 2D image point $\tilde{\mathbf{u}} = [u, v, 1]^\top$ through a $3 \times 3$ planar homography matrix $\mathbf{H}$:\index{Zhang's calibration!homography matrix}\index{Camera calibration!absolute conic}
$$
s \begin{bmatrix} u \\ v \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \mathbf{K} \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{r}_1 & \mathbf{r}_2 & \mathbf{r}_3 & \mathbf{t} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} X \\ Y \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \mathbf{K} \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{r}_1 & \mathbf{r}_2 & \mathbf{t} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} X \\ Y \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \mathbf{H} \begin{bmatrix} X \\ Y \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}
$$
where $\mathbf{H} = [\mathbf{h}_1 \; \mathbf{h}_2 \; \mathbf{h}_3] = \lambda \mathbf{K} [\mathbf{r}_1 \; \mathbf{r}_2 \; \mathbf{t}]$ with arbitrary nonzero scalar $\lambda$.

#### Orthogonality constraints on the absolute conic

Because the rotation vectors $\mathbf{r}_1$ and $\mathbf{r}_2$ are orthonormal columns of an $SO(3)$ matrix ($\mathbf{r}_1^\top \mathbf{r}_2 = 0$ and $\|\mathbf{r}_1\| = \|\mathbf{r}_2\| = 1$), inverting $\mathbf{K}$ yields:
$$
\mathbf{r}_1 = \frac{1}{\lambda} \mathbf{K}^{-1} \mathbf{h}_1, \quad \mathbf{r}_2 = \frac{1}{\lambda} \mathbf{K}^{-1} \mathbf{h}_2
$$
Imposing orthonormality on $\mathbf{r}_1$ and $\mathbf{r}_2$ defines two fundamental algebraic constraints per homography:
$$
\mathbf{h}_1^\top \mathbf{K}^{-\top} \mathbf{K}^{-1} \mathbf{h}_2 = 0
$$
$$
\mathbf{h}_1^\top \mathbf{K}^{-\top} \mathbf{K}^{-1} \mathbf{h}_1 - \mathbf{h}_2^\top \mathbf{K}^{-\top} \mathbf{K}^{-1} \mathbf{h}_2 = 0
$$
The symmetric matrix $\mathbf{B} = \mathbf{K}^{-\top} \mathbf{K}^{-1}$ represents the image of the absolute conic (IAC):
$$
\mathbf{B} = \begin{bmatrix} B_{11} & B_{12} & B_{13} \\ B_{12} & B_{22} & B_{23} \\ B_{13} & B_{23} & B_{33} \end{bmatrix}
$$
Defining the 6-vector $\mathbf{b} = [B_{11}, B_{12}, B_{22}, B_{13}, B_{23}, B_{33}]^\top$, each quadratic term $\mathbf{h}_i^\top \mathbf{B} \mathbf{h}_j$ can be rewritten as the linear inner product $\mathbf{v}_{ij}^\top \mathbf{b}$, where:
$$
\mathbf{v}_{ij} = \begin{bmatrix} h_{i1}h_{j1} \\ h_{i1}h_{j2} + h_{i2}h_{j1} \\ h_{i2}h_{j2} \\ h_{i3}h_{j1} + h_{i1}h_{j3} \\ h_{i3}h_{j2} + h_{i2}h_{j3} \\ h_{i3}h_{j3} \end{bmatrix}
$$
The two constraints per observed orientation become the linear system:
$$
\begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{v}_{12}^\top \\ (\mathbf{v}_{11} - \mathbf{v}_{22})^\top \end{bmatrix} \mathbf{b} = \mathbf{0}
$$
Stacking $N \ge 3$ images forms the homogeneous system $\mathbf{V} \mathbf{b} = \mathbf{0}$, where $\mathbf{V} \in \mathbb{R}^{2N \times 6}$. The right singular vector of $\mathbf{V}$ corresponding to the smallest singular value provides $\mathbf{b}$ up to a scale factor. The intrinsic parameters $(f_x, f_y, c_x, c_y)$ and skew $\gamma$ are then uniquely extracted via Cholesky factorization of $\mathbf{B}$. This closed-form linear solution initializes the non-linear Levenberg–Marquardt optimization minimizing reprojection residuals over all observed fiducial corners.

## Kinematic Stopping Envelopes and Information Age Lag {#sec-appendix-systems-stopping}

In distributed systems, pipeline latency represents elapsed waiting time or queuing delay. In physical AI, end-to-end software latency converts directly into irreversible physical displacement—uninspected "blind travel"—during which an embodied machine traverses space with undiminished momentum before actuators can begin retarding motion. Halting an embodied machine transporting mass $m$ at velocity $v$ requires balancing sensorimotor information freshness, neural compute budgets, and fieldbus dispatch against physical mechanical braking deceleration.

### Sensorimotor information age and lag distance

For a specified hazard detector and stop path, let $\tau_{\text{delay}}$ bound the time from the physical state represented by the evidence until validated braking deceleration begins:\index{Kinematic stopping distance!observation age}
$$ \tau_{\text{delay}} = t_{\text{age}} + t_{\text{detect}} + t_{\text{compute}} + T_{\text{bus}} + T_{\text{act}} $$
where:

- $t_{\text{age}}$ converts the evidence timestamp to the controller clock and includes exposure/readout and clock error.
- $t_{\text{detect}}$ bounds recognition or lease-expiry detection.
- $t_{\text{compute}}$ is the admitted stop decision, including any required input transfer.
- $T_{\text{bus}}$ bounds command dispatch and network queuing.
- $T_{\text{act}}$ ends when the measured actuator begins delivering the specified deceleration, not when a command register is written.

Under the explicit simplifying assumption that speed cannot increase before brake onset, the blind travel is bounded by $d_{\text{blind}}=v\,\tau_{\text{delay}}$. If propulsion or a slope can increase speed, use its validated acceleration bound in this interval instead.

### Braking dynamics and friction limits

Tire-floor friction and actuator torque place upper limits on achievable deceleration; $a\le\mu g$ does not establish what braking the machine will deliver.\index{Braking!friction limit} Let $a_{\text{brake}}>0$ be a validated lower bound on *achieved* deceleration throughout the stop, for the declared load, temperature, slope, brake condition, and surface. A justified friction floor $\mu_{\text{floor}}$ may support that bound, but does not replace brake tests. With constant or stronger braking after onset, a localization bound $\delta_{\text{loc}}$, a fixed protective clearance $\delta_{\text{margin}}$, and a tracking-error bound $\epsilon_{\text{track}}$,
$$ d_{\text{stop}}(v)=v\,\tau_{\text{delay}}+\frac{v^2}{2a_{\text{brake}}}+\delta_{\text{loc}}+\delta_{\text{margin}}+\epsilon_{\text{track}}. $$
Motion is admitted only when $d_{\text{stop}}(v)\le D_{\text{clear}}$, where $D_{\text{clear}}$ is taken as a validated lower bound on available path clearance. This is the inset stopping distance that @sec-enforcement-stopping-envelopes defends. The sampled controller must reserve intersample travel and a state-matched stop before the viable region is lost.

### Kinetic energy derating and friction collapse

In an ideal friction-limited model, lowering $\mu$ from $\mu_{\text{nom}}$ to a positive $\mu_{\text{fault}}$ changes the braking-distance ratio to $\mu_{\text{nom}}/\mu_{\text{fault}}$.\index{Velocity clamp!kinetic derating} That ratio is illustrative; actual deceleration can also be limited by brake hardware or control. If surface friction is not sensed in time, derive $a_{\text{brake}}$ from a controlled surface condition and inspection schedule, exclude degraded surfaces, or withhold motion. For the constant-speed pre-brake model above, solving the clearance inequality gives
$$ v_{\text{clamp}}=-a_{\text{brake}}\tau_{\text{delay}}+\sqrt{(a_{\text{brake}}\tau_{\text{delay}})^2+2a_{\text{brake}}\left(D_{\text{clear}}-\delta_{\text{loc}}-\delta_{\text{margin}}-\epsilon_{\text{track}}\right)}. $$
This clamp is valid only when $D_{\text{clear}}$ exceeds the three fixed allowances, the braking and timing lower bounds hold, and the speed bound is enforced before entering the hazard corridor. No positive clamp follows if the available deceleration floor is unknown or zero.

## Wire Formats for the Record Chain {#sec-appendix-systems-wire-formats}

In distributed machine learning systems, inter-service contracts are defined via serialization frameworks such as Protocol Buffers, FlatBuffers, or JSON schemas, which rely on variable-length wire formats, dynamic deserialization, pointer indirection, and heap allocation. In physical AI systems, however, records crossing the causal boundary between unprivileged deep learning runtimes (executing in user space under Linux on 64-bit application processors) and certified real-time safety monitors (executing on 32-bit lockstep microcontrollers or RTOS partitions) must satisfy strict embedded systems invariants:\index{Serialization!wire formats}\index{Memory layout!natural alignment}\index{Zero-allocation!embedded contract chain}\index{Safety contract chain!14-record lineage}
1. *Zero Dynamic Allocation*: Deserialization must never invoke dynamic memory managers (`malloc`, `free`, C++ `new`, `delete`). Dynamic allocators suffer from heap fragmentation, unbounded bucket-search times, and global allocator mutex contention that violate hard real-time deadlines. All record slots, mailbox staging areas, and scratch buffers must be statically sized at compile time and preallocated in dedicated static SRAM or Data Tightly Coupled Memory (DTCM) pools.
2. *Deterministic Parse Time*: Wire formats must eliminate variable-length pointer chasing. Fields must reside at fixed, deterministic byte offsets, allowing validation logic to inspect bounds and timestamps in $\mathcal{O}(1)$ time with cycle-bounded instruction counts.
3. *Natural Alignment Across Heterogeneous ABIs*: On heterogeneous SoCs combining 64-bit application processors (ARM Cortex-A or x86_64) and 32-bit real-time microcontrollers (ARM Cortex-R52 or Cortex-M7), data types must be naturally aligned. A scalar of size $k$ bytes must reside at an offset satisfying:
$$ \text{offset} \equiv 0 \pmod k $$
Specifically, 64-bit timestamps and integers (`uint64_t`, `float64`) align on 8-byte boundaries ($k=8$), 32-bit values (`uint32_t`, `float32`) align on 4-byte boundaries ($k=4$), and 16-bit integers (`uint16_t`) align on 2-byte boundaries ($k=2$). If a data structure violates natural alignment, 32-bit microcontrollers configured with strict alignment checking raise hardware data abort exceptions (`UsageFault`). Even when unaligned accesses are supported in hardware, the memory subsystem splits the load or store into multiple bus transactions, destroying the single-cycle memory atomicity required by lock-free seqlocks. Furthermore, if fields are misaligned, compilers automatically insert invisible, architecture-dependent padding bytes, producing binary layout discrepancies between 64-bit and 32-bit compilers. By declaring all padding explicitly as `reserved` zero-filled bytes, the wire formats guarantee identical bit-level memory layouts across all compilers and processor cores.

**The 14-Record Safety Contract Chain.** Across this book, the physical AI machine stack maintains an unbroken chain of 14 formal cyber-physical contracts that govern execution from raw electromechanics up to legal release certification:

1. *Body Limit Record* (Contract 1, Body): Declares physical electromechanical envelopes (peak currents, torque limits, thermal $I^2 t$ constants, bus voltage limits, and gear ratios; @sec-body-actuator-limits).
2. *Proposal Record* (Contract 2, Brain): Emits candidate unprivileged kinematic trajectory setpoints across the proposal boundary (@sec-brain, @sec-appendix-systems-wire-header).
3. *Transport Budget / Handoff Record* (Contract 3, Nervous System): Specifies network cadences, clock domains, and sensor aging budgets ($\mathcal{H}_1$) across heterogeneous compute nodes (@sec-nervous-handoffs-matrix).
4. *Demonstration Provenance Record* (Contract 4, Data): Binds physical data collection conditions, sensor calibration revisions, plant serial numbers, and scenario ledgers to training datasets (@sec-data-policy-coverage).
5. *Policy Manifest* (Contract 5, Training): Cryptographically binds model architecture, quantization precision, network weight digests, and training distribution bounds (@sec-training-policy-manifest).
6. *Evaluation Record* (Contract 6, Evaluation): Summarizes statistical qualification trials across the operational design domain (ODD) and configures runtime monitor specifications (@sec-evaluation).
7. *Perception Evidence Record* (Contract 7, Perception): Encapsulates sensor observations with hardware capture epochs, clock conversion bounds, and spatial unprojection covariances (@sec-perception).
8. *Scene Memory State Record* (Contract 8, Memory): Maintains persistent spatial beliefs, tracked object bounds, volumetric occupancy fields, and invalidation deadlines across occlusions (@sec-memory).
9. *Intent Specification / Lease* (Contract 9, Intent): Formalizes admitted semantic goals, task tolerance boxes, wrench limits, and execution lease horizons (@sec-intent, @sec-appendix-systems-wire-intent).
10. *Trajectory Contract / Plan Record* (Contract 10, Planning): Packages admitted dynamic splines, knot point cadences, commit deadlines ($t_{\text{commit}}$), and emergency stop suffixes (@sec-planning, @sec-appendix-systems-wire-trajectory).
11. *Admitted Command Record / Enforcement Record* (Contract 11, Enforcement): Emits verified execution tokens, Control Barrier Function margins ($h(\mathbf{x})$), and tracking error ceilings ($\epsilon_{\text{track}}$) to actuator drives (@sec-enforcement, @sec-appendix-systems-wire-enforcement).
12. *Placement Record / Deployment Envelope* (Contract 12, Placement): Documents execution core affinities, memory interconnect QoS arbitration, loaded WCET bounds, and hardware isolation invariants (@sec-placement, @sec-appendix-systems-wire-placement).
13. *Authority Record / Forensic Log* (Contract 13, Intervention): Logs operator handover commands, bumpless transfer blending coefficients ($\alpha$), and tamper-evident cryptographic hash chains (@sec-intervention, @sec-appendix-systems-wire-authority).
14. *Verification Matrix / Release Manifest* (Contract 14, Verification & Release): Provides signed cryptographic attestation binding hardware root of trust anchors, adjudicator verdicts, fault injection trial ledgers, and residual-claims registers (@sec-verification, @sec-release, @sec-appendix-systems-wire-release).

Online runtime records (Contracts 2, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, and 13) travel across high-frequency shared SRAM mailboxes and real-time fieldbuses, requiring fixed-size layouts and zero dynamic allocation. Configuration and offline assurance artifacts (Contracts 1, 3, 4, 5, 6, 12, and 14) are bound cryptographically by SHA-256 digests of their canonical binary encodings. All records use standard little-endian byte ordering for multi-byte scalars (`uint64_t`, `uint32_t`, `uint16_t`, `float32`, `float64`). Lineage is established by embedding parent SHA-256 digests, runtime corruption is caught via IEEE 802.3 CRC-32 checksums over headers and payloads, and operator authority is authenticated via HMAC-SHA-256 and Ed25519 digital signatures. Offline records (placement, fault, release) are identified by the SHA-256 digest of their canonical encoding, and the record that consumes one stores that digest under the consumed record's name.

### Proposal header and chunk payload {#sec-appendix-systems-wire-header}

Every proposal that crosses the proposal boundary opens with the same header, and `payload_kind` selects the payload that follows at `0x50`. @Tbl-appendix-systems-wire-header lays out the header with the minimal chunk payload of @sec-nervous-cadences. The chunk carries kinematic setpoints only. Torque is computed on the permission side, where the tracker derives it from the admitted reference, so a learned proposal never names a motor torque.

| Offset                 | Field              | Scalar type       | Unit                 | Invariant and check                                                                                          |
|:-----------------------|:-------------------|:------------------|:---------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `0x00`                 | `sequence_id`      | `uint64_t`        | dimensionless        | Strictly increasing per producer; a record not newer than the last accepted one is rejected.                 |
| `0x08`                 | `t_evidence_ns`    | `uint64_t`        | ns, permission clock | Capture epoch of the oldest evidence the proposal rests on, converted to the safety microcontroller's clock. |
| `0x10`                 | `t_issue_ns`       | `uint64_t`        | ns, permission clock | Time the producer published the record.                                                                      |
| `0x18`                 | `t_expire_ns`      | `uint64_t`        | ns, permission clock | Requested absolute expiry, no later than the chunk lease allows; the permission path may only shorten it.    |
| `0x20`                 | `frame_id`         | `uint64_t`        | dimensionless        | Transform-tree key and calibration revision of the setpoints' frame.                                         |
| `0x28`                 | `parent_digest`    | `uint8_t[32]`     | SHA-256              | Digest of the record this proposal was derived from; establishes lineage, authenticates nothing.             |
| `0x48`                 | `sync_error_ns`    | `uint32_t`        | ns                   | Bound on the evidence time's conversion error; added to every age the reader checks.                         |
| `0x4C`                 | `payload_kind`     | `uint16_t`        | enumeration          | `CHUNK` for this payload; `INTENT`, `TRAJECTORY`, and `OPERATOR` select the other payloads.                  |
| `0x4E`                 | `payload_len`      | `uint16_t`        | bytes                | Payload length; bounds the parser before any payload byte is read.                                           |
| `0x50`                 | `num_waypoints`    | `uint16_t`        | count                | Chunk horizon $K$; a count outside the configured range is rejected.                                         |
| `0x52`                 | `num_joints`       | `uint8_t`         | count                | Commanded joints $N_j$; must equal the configured count, and `payload_len` must equal $4+8KN_j$.             |
| `0x53`                 | reserved           | `uint8_t`         | —                    | Zero.                                                                                                        |
| `0x54`                 | `joint_positions`  | `float32[K][N_j]` | rad                  | Commanded joint angles within the reach limits ($q_{\min} \le q \le q_{\max}$).                              |
| `0x54` + $4KN_j$       | `joint_velocities` | `float32[K][N_j]` | rad/s                | Commanded joint velocities within certified ceilings ($\lVert \dot{\mathbf{q}} \rVert \le \dot{q}_{\max}$).  |
| `0x50` + `payload_len` | `crc32`            | `uint32_t`        | checksum             | Last field; IEEE 802.3 CRC-32 over all preceding bytes.                                                      |

: **Proposal header and chunk payload**: Field offsets, scalar types, units, and invariants for a chunk proposal exchanged through the seqlock mailbox of @algo-lock-free-trajectory. The header occupies `0x00`–`0x4F` in every proposal; the other payload layouts in this section begin at `0x50`. {#tbl-appendix-systems-wire-header tbl-colwidths="[14,17,14,14,41]"}

### Intent payload {#sec-appendix-systems-wire-intent}

The intent lease of @sec-intent-lease travels under the proposal header with `payload_kind` set to `INTENT` (@tbl-appendix-systems-wire-intent). Three header fields take specific meanings. `t_evidence_ns` is the parent belief record's evidence epoch, never its estimate epoch; `parent_digest` is that belief record's digest, which the permission path matches against a retained record; and `t_expire_ns` is the requested expiry, which the permission path shortens to the earliest of the evidence horizon, its configured lease ceiling, and the stop deadline. The six `bounds` values are three conservative position-error envelopes and three task tolerances in the base frame named by `frame_id`. They are not an encoding of a covariance, and the producer must justify any conversion from its covariance estimate, including calibration bias and the declared tail risk.

| Offset        | Field              | Scalar type  | Unit               | Invariant and check                                                                                                               |
|:--------------|:-------------------|:-------------|:-------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `0x00`–`0x4F` | proposal header    | as above     | as above           | @tbl-appendix-systems-wire-header, with `payload_kind` = `INTENT`.                                                                |
| `0x50`        | `target_pose`      | `float64[7]` | m; unit quaternion | Base-frame position and orientation; finite values, normalized quaternion, workspace prefilter.                                   |
| `0x88`        | `bounds`           | `float32[6]` | m                  | Error envelope $e_{x,y,z}$, then task tolerance $r_{x,y,z}$; $0 \le e_i \le r_i$, each checked against the approved task profile. |
| `0xA0`        | `wrench_request`   | `float32[6]` | N; N·m             | Three requested forces and three torques; clamped or rejected against independent task and actuator limits.                       |
| `0xB8`        | `terminal_request` | `uint32_t`   | enumeration        | Requested terminal mode; the permission path selects a feasible approved response from the current load and contact state.        |
| `0xBC`        | `crc32`            | `uint32_t`   | checksum           | IEEE 802.3 CRC-32 over all preceding bytes.                                                                                       |

: **Intent payload**: The intent lease as a proposal-header payload. Orientation tolerances and contact-mode rules come from an independently approved task profile; the quaternion is the proposed orientation only. {#tbl-appendix-systems-wire-intent tbl-colwidths="[13,17,13,15,42]"}

### Trajectory payload {#sec-appendix-systems-wire-trajectory}

The trajectory record of @sec-planning-trajectory-contract replaces the chunk on the running machine and travels under the same proposal header, with `payload_kind` set to `TRAJECTORY` and `parent_digest` set to the digest of the active intent lease (@tbl-appendix-systems-wire-trajectory). The header's `t_expire_ns` carries the chunk lease; the intent's own expiry comes from the lease that `parent_digest` identifies. The setpoint samples and the assumptions sidecar travel outside this fixed part. The permission path verifies `sidecar_digest` over both, validates the complete candidate in staging memory, and latches the admitted setpoints and stop suffix in protected memory before tracking begins.

| Offset           | Field              | Scalar type       | Unit                 | Invariant and check                                                                                              |
|:-----------------|:-------------------|:------------------|:---------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `0x00`–`0x4F`    | proposal header    | as above          | as above             | @tbl-appendix-systems-wire-header, with `payload_kind` = `TRAJECTORY`.                                           |
| `0x50`           | `sample_period_ns` | `uint32_t`        | ns                   | Setpoint cadence $\Delta t_{\text{step}}$; must match the configured decoder.                                    |
| `0x54`           | `num_samples`      | `uint16_t`        | count                | Nominal setpoints in the digested sample payload; bounds its size.                                               |
| `0x56`           | `num_joints`       | `uint8_t`         | count                | Commanded joints $N_j$; must equal the configured count.                                                         |
| `0x57`           | `payload_version`  | `uint8_t`         | enumeration          | Decoder version; an unknown version is rejected.                                                                 |
| `0x58`           | `t_start_ns`       | `uint64_t`        | ns, permission clock | First nominal sample.                                                                                            |
| `0x60`           | `t_commit_ns`      | `uint64_t`        | ns, permission clock | Latest entry into the matched stop suffix; $t_{\text{commit}}=t_{\text{stop\_end}}-T_{\text{stop}}$.             |
| `0x68`           | `t_plan_exp_ns`    | `uint64_t`        | ns, permission clock | End of the nominal setpoints.                                                                                    |
| `0x70`           | `t_stop_end_ns`    | `uint64_t`        | ns, permission clock | Protected stop completion; $t_{\text{start}}\le t_{\text{commit}}<t_{\text{plan\_exp}}<t_{\text{stop\_end}}$.    |
| `0x78`           | `sidecar_digest`   | `uint8_t[32]`     | SHA-256              | Digest over the setpoint samples and the assumptions sidecar; binds content.                                     |
| `0x98`           | `seam_state`       | `float32[3][N_j]` | rad; rad/s; rad/s²   | Entry state $(q,\dot q,\ddot q)$ of each joint.                                                                  |
| `0x98` + $12N_j$ | `stop_suffix`      | `float32[6][N_j]` | quintic coefficients | One quintic stop per joint; must be resident and feasible from every state reachable before $t_{\text{commit}}$. |
| `0x98` + $36N_j$ | `crc32`            | `uint32_t`        | checksum             | IEEE 802.3 CRC-32 over all preceding bytes.                                                                      |

: **Trajectory payload**: The trajectory record as a proposal-header payload. The four deadlines are absolute times on the safety microcontroller's clock; the variable-length setpoint samples and the assumptions sidecar are bound by `sidecar_digest` and validated before activation. {#tbl-appendix-systems-wire-trajectory tbl-colwidths="[14,16,14,15,41]"}

### Enforcement record {#sec-appendix-systems-wire-enforcement}

The enforcement record of @sec-enforcement-telemetry is configuration, not a proposal, so it carries no proposal header (@tbl-appendix-systems-wire-enforcement). Three digests name what the record rests on: the evaluation record, the limit records behind the stopping envelope, and the validity region. Each threshold names the fallback-ladder rung that a failed check selects. Where the rung depends on whether the body is moving, the row names both, `STOP` in motion and `HOLD` at standstill. A proposal refused while the active lease holds selects no rung, because the setpoints already admitted stay in force until that lease lapses.

| Offset               | Field                      | Scalar type       | Unit                                 | Check, and the rung a failure selects                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
|:---------------------|:---------------------------|:------------------|:-------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `0x00`               | `evaluation_record_digest` | `uint8_t[32]`     | SHA-256                              | Evaluation record whose runtime monitor specifications become this record's monitor channels.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
| `0x20`               | `limit_record_digest`      | `uint8_t[32]`     | SHA-256                              | Canonical list of the limit records whose braking, onset, and actuator limits parameterize $d_{\text{stop}}(v)$.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| `0x40`               | `validity_region_digest`   | `uint8_t[32]`     | SHA-256                              | `validity_region`, the plant-parameter bounds the thresholds rest on. On the mobile manipulator it covers the arm at the door, where it equals the target ODD, and at the packing station through the mug pick and the handover approach. Each base configuration, normal or restricted, loads as its own enforcement record, so this field holds the region digest of that configuration and its friction premise. A live state outside it that the machine observes selects `STOP`. |
| `0x60`               | `loop_period_ns`           | `uint32_t`        | ns                                   | Permission-loop period $T_{\text{loop}}$; the placement record's `nominal_period_ns` must equal it.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |

A proposal whose upper evidence age exceeds it is refused, and the permission path shortens `t_expire_ns` to at most `t_evidence_ns` plus the ceiling minus `sync_error_ns`. A proposal whose `sequence_id` is not newer is refused; an expired lease selects `STOP` in motion and `HOLD` at standstill.                                                                 |
